title: ow to watch the 2026 Atlanta Falcons: TV listings for Kevin Stefanski's first season The Atlanta Falcons have a new head coach and a lot of uncertainty at quarterback. Here's how to watch all 17 games this year. Takashi Williams 2
summary:
Two-time NFL Coach of the Year Kevin Stefanski is now in Atlanta, with another shaky QB situation on his hands. Rich Storry / Imagn Images via Reuters Connect
The 2026 NFL season marks a painful anniversary for the Atlanta Falcons. It’s now been 10 seasons since their heartbreaking defeat in Super Bowl LI. In that time, the Dirty Birds have returned to the playoffs just once.
In the midst of their eight-year absence from postseason football, massive sweeps in the Falcons’ front office took place
full_text:
Two-time NFL Coach of the Year Kevin Stefanski is now in Atlanta, with another shaky QB situation on his hands. Rich Storry / Imagn Images via Reuters Connect
The 2026 NFL season marks a painful anniversary for the Atlanta Falcons. It’s now been 10 seasons since their heartbreaking defeat in Super Bowl LI. In that time, the Dirty Birds have returned to the playoffs just once.
In the midst of their eight-year absence from postseason football, massive sweeps in the Falcons’ front office took place. Matt Ryan , the MVP-winning quarterback from that Super Bowl runner-up 2016 team, is the president of football for the franchise. Ian Cunningham is the new general manager. Two-time NFL Coach of the Year Kevin Stefanski is now in charge, and Tommy Rees is his offensive coordinator.
They’ll be supported by first-team All-Pro running back Bijan Robinson, field-stretching receiver Drake London and standout tight end Kyle Pitts. But a major point of contention remains around the quarterback position, similar to the situation Stefanski had with the Cleveland Browns.
Who will be Stefanski’s starter? Will it be a weathered Tua Tagovailoa, coming off one of his worst professional seasons? Or a potentially riskier, more intriguing option in Michael Penix Jr., who underwent surgery for a partially torn ACL that ended his 2025 campaign? And will Stefanski at some point this year have to turn to undrafted rookie Jack Strand ?
Whatever happens under center, this will be an interesting season to watch unfold in Atlanta. Unfortunately with broadcast changes and streaming exclusivity, it’s only gotten harder to tune in to the NFL. Our guide will help you catch all 17 regular-season Falcons games in 2026. And don’t forget to follow the Falcons and Georgia native Josh Kendall on The Athletic for year-round coverage.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, the man who helped deliver the 28-3 comeback to crush Falcons fans everywhere. Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen, while Amin is partnered with newcomer and recent Hall of Fame inductee Drew Brees. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The Falcons appear on MNF once, in Week 4 when they visit the hated New Orleans Saints; it airs on ESPN only. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Matt Ryan to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the pregame and postgame personalities are Falcons legend and Hall of Famer Tony Gonzalez, Richard Sherman and Andrew Whitworth.

full_text:
Carolina has been bringing along Darren Waller slowly since signing him in mid-August. Matt Kelley / Getty Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — The Carolina Panthers raised some eyebrows in NFL circles this week by keeping five tight ends on their initial roster. But it didn’t really come as a shock to Tommy Tremble, who joked that the team could run “05 personnel” with all five tight ends on the field with quarterback Bryce Young.
“Everyone has a different aspect to their game, so it wasn’t very surprising to us. If anything, it shows what they think about us,” said Tremble, the sixth-year tight end. “So after that deadline hit, to see them keep five of us, it was kind of reassuring for us.”
Keeping five on the 53-man roster doesn’t mean the Panthers will have all five active on game days. Head coach Dave Canales said there are still “some things to work out” in terms of how the tight ends impact the game-day math.
The Panthers had trade talks involving Ja’Tavion Sanders before Sunday’s roster cuts, according to a league source who wasn’t authorized to discuss the discussions. Maybe a team that’s light at tight end or sustains an injury at the position calls general manager Dan Morgan about Sanders, a fourth-round pick from Texas in 2024.
But for the time being, the Panthers are rolling with five tight ends, one fewer than the six wide receivers who made the team.
“Right now we’re committed. Not to say that something couldn’t change. I don’t know what the future holds,” Morgan said of the TE group. “But I know coach Canales has a plan for each and every one of those guys. What he does with them on game day is yet to be seen. But right now we feel good about it.”
The tight end room became crowded two weeks ago after Morgan signed free agent Darren Waller , who caught 24 passes, including six touchdowns. last year for Miami but missed seven games due to injuries.
Waller, who turns 34 the day of the season opener against the Chicago Bears, dealt with three injuries last season, including a torn quad early in training camp after he ended a one-year retirement.
Since signing Waller to a one-year deal for the veteran minimum Aug. 17, the Panthers have brought him along at a snail’s pace: He’s only caught one pass during an 11-on-11 drill and worked with trainers on the side Tuesday as part of what Canales called normal maintenance.
But Canales conceded that questions about Waller’s health impacted the decision to go with five tight ends. “Definitely a part of it. Guys that we trust being here. But then also we’ve gotta see how Darren handles a full volume of a week,” Canales said. “How does he come out and respond off of a game week? We need to gather that information as we go.”
The Panthers believe each of the tight ends adds a little different flavor to the offense. Canales views Tremble as a versatile athlete physical enough to help in the run game and fast enough to stretch the field. He sees the second-year Mitchell Evans as “a big, traditional” inline tight end, and called Feleipe Franks one of the premiere special teams players in the NFL.
Sanders and Waller have similar skill sets as receiving-first tight ends, which is why observers viewed Sanders as the odd man out — despite the fact that the former Texas standout was the Panthers’ leading receiver among TEs the past two seasons.
Sanders hauled in 33 passes for 342 yards and a touchdown as a rookie in 2024, when his production dipped after he sustained a neck injury after being upended by Trent McDuffie in a Week 11 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. He missed four games last year with a pair of ankle injuries, including a season-ending fracture in Week 17 against the Seattle Seahawks.
The knocks on Sanders have been his blocking and special teams play. The Panthers gave Sanders ample opportunity to improve the latter by playing him on several special teams units during the preseason.
“JT’s shown he can be a really good special teams player, along with giving us receiving ability in the pass game,” Morgan said. “So JT definitely has a lot of traits that we like and he’s productive on teams as well. So he definitely has a lot of value for us.”
Conversely, Franks is a special teams demon who has sharpened his receiving skills since first joining the Panthers two years ago.
“He’s a dog, man. I love Feleipe,” Tremble said of the former Florida quarterback. “The way he’s come in to work and just be the best he can be, it’s so fun seeing — especially when he first got here in ’24 — his development as a tight end, as a player, as a teammate — it’s out of this world, man. He’s a really good football player.”
The X-factor in all of this is Waller. The former Georgia Tech wideout is fairly far removed from his back-to-back 1,100-yard receiving seasons with the Raiders in 2019-20, but showed last year he can still be a matchup problem when healthy.
The Panthers don’t have any other tight ends who look like the 6-6, 238-pound Waller, who is more of a slot receiver. After wearing No. 35 his first two weeks, Waller now has a number (88) more befitting a tight end. Assuming his body holds up, you have to believe Waller will have a jersey on Sundays.
“We know what he looks like on film. We know the element he can bring to us,” Canales said. “So some things to work out there to see who we’re gonna have up helping us on game day. But a group that I feel really strongly about.”

title: Bears GM Ryan Poles: Line depth led to moving on from Day 2 draft picks We heard from Poles after the team made its cuts and he explained why the roster allowed him to move on from recent picks. Kevin Fishbain 13
summary:
The Bears' depth at defensive tackle, including Neville Gallimore, right, made Gervon Dexter expendable. Steve Roberts / Imagn Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — No general manager or head coach has ever publicly said constructing a 53-man roster is easy, but this is the first time Chicago Bears GM Ryan Poles has made final cuts after a playoff appearance.
“As you get a more talented roster, it gets really difficult to make those tough decisions,” he said Tuesday. “… I love the depth. I love the talent.
full_text:
The Bears' depth at defensive tackle, including Neville Gallimore, right, made Gervon Dexter expendable. Steve Roberts / Imagn Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — No general manager or head coach has ever publicly said constructing a 53-man roster is easy, but this is the first time Chicago Bears GM Ryan Poles has made final cuts after a playoff appearance.
“As you get a more talented roster, it gets really difficult to make those tough decisions,” he said Tuesday. “… I love the depth. I love the talent. This is probably the most versatile roster we’ve had, guys being able to play different positions, which I think is going to really serve us well as we get into the season.”
Poles remembered a couple of years ago when, as the season was about to begin, he was still trying to figure out the center position and the backup. The offensive line is deep. Poles is proud of the interior six. But questions remain about the defense, injured players and left tackle.
The biggest question remains unanswered: cornerback Kyler Gordon’s status .
Here are five takeaways from the Bears GM’s Tuesday news conference.
Gervon Dexter has been an annual “breakout candidate.” This year’s storyline focused on it being the final year of his rookie contract, creating extra motivation.
Not only did Dexter not have a standout camp, but the players the Bears brought in exceeded expectations, leading to his trade to Atlanta .
“That deal was more about timing than anything. Timing and fit,” Poles said. “You know, we had some young guys really pushing that came in this year with Jordan (van den Berg) and (Jayden) Loving. They did a really good job, and we felt like it was a good fit as we moved forward.”
Dexter was drafted for Matt Eberflus’ defense. He did lead interior linemen in sacks last season, but clearly coordinator Dennis Allen has other preferences.
“It really has to do with the room. That room was highly competitive,” Poles said. “Those young guys started making a push when we got through camp, and along with obviously Grady (Jarrett), (Kentavius) Street and Neville (Gallimore). And we felt like the timing made sense for us. So really it was about the shape in the room and really how well those young guys were doing, too. So we feel really good and confident in our talent level at that position.”
Coach Ben Johnson said last week he felt that the defensive tackle group had been underrated outside the building. It won’t be hard for these guys to stop the run better than last year’s group did, but can they get to the passer more effectively than Dexter did? Getting more from Dayo Odeyingbo on the interior, plus the ascent of van den Berg, creates some confidence.
There’s no sense putting a timeline on the Bears’ second-year tackle, considering he blew away any expectation in his return from a torn patellar tendon.
In the spring, no one thought he’d be practicing by now. Now we flip the page to: when can he play in games?
Getting Trapilo in team drills in padded practices will be key, Poles said, so that the offensive tackle can test his anchor and mobility.
“There’s definitely rust to knock off,” Poles said. “I don’t know how long that’ll take before he’s involved with the game plan and starting or a rotational guy or active. It’s too early to tell right now.”
Padded practices start to decrease significantly when the season gets underway, which adds to the significance of Trapilo’s return, since he’s been able to be in full pads already for a couple of weeks.
“In helmets, or not even helmets, it looks fabulous, or he wouldn’t be where he is,” Poles said. “But he’s playing football.”
The Eagles signed left tackle Kiran Amegadjie to their practice squad Tuesday, ending his time with the Bears. A third-round pick in 2024, Amegadjie played in six games with one forgettable start under brutal conditions in Minnesota.
“I would go back to the (offensive line) room and the competition,” Poles said. “I had a good conversation with him at the end. It really just wasn’t a level of consistency that we were looking for.”
The Trapilo injury first opened the door for Amegadjie to earn a role on the team, and then when Braxton Jones had to miss a week, that meant Amegadjie could play with the starters. But he didn’t play well enough with the opportunities.
Poles noted that the front office has been “pretty quick” to be honest about a player not working out and then moving on. Among seven second- and third-round picks from 2022-24, only cornerback Tyrique Stevenson is on the active roster, as Gordon is on the physically unable to perform list.
Safety Jaquan Brisker exited via free agency and Dexter was traded, but defensive tackle Zacch Pickens, receiver/returner Velus Jones and now Amegadjie were cut.
The production from those rounds hasn’t been strong, though Poles pointed out two things — their top picks are performing well. Right tackle Darnell Wright earned a contract extension and Caleb Williams, Rome Odunze and Colston Loveland have bright futures.
And Poles also wanted to highlight the success they’ve had in the late rounds and with undrafted rookies.
“Kyle (Monangai), UDFAs like Tyson (Bagent), Theo (Benedet), Jahdae (Walker). So I think we’ve done a really good job,” he said. “But we do research on (picks who don’t work out), and we look into it. You have to be honest with yourself with what works and what doesn’t work. You just keep tightening the screws on your process.”
Multiple things can be true. Poles and the scouting staff haven’t had a good enough hit rate on Day 2. But they have also helped construct a roster that won 11 games last year and has playoff expectations this season.
The 2025 second-round pick, who tore his ACL last season, seems to be trending in the right direction. Poles spoke much more positively about his outlook than Gordon’s, for comparison purposes.
“He’s already doing position work off to the side,” he said. “We’ll simulate some individual and practice-type things to get him prepared mentally and physically, and his endurance needs to continue to improve. But he’s working his butt off. I would imagine him being back at some point here when he gets through this little last phase of his rehab.”
Poles and Bears coaches have praised what they saw from Turner when he moved to defensive end, but he appeared in only five games and had two tackles for loss. The new rules for players on the PUP list mean Turner can begin practicing after Week 2.
“Knocking that rust off and becoming a football player, starting to get that short-area quickness and really being able to react and have the instincts come back,” Poles said. “Especially playing defensive line, you’re getting hit from every different direction. … When that happens it’ll be great and we’ll get him back out there, but I’m not exactly sure of when that all is going to occur.”
Poles was able to get a draft pick and a player in return for Dexter. The Falcons sent 2023 fourth-round cornerback Clark Phillips to Chicago, adding depth to a position that has had a bunch of injuries this summer.
“We like, from the tape that we watched, his man coverage skills,” Poles said. “Short-area quickness is really good, speed is really good, sticky in coverage.”
While Phillips played predominantly outside corner with the Falcons, he played slot corner in college, and Poles said he liked that tape, too.
With Malik Muhammad slated to start as the nickel corner, that opens the door for Phillips to be the top reserve on the outside.

title: NFL execs rank NFC teams: Rams, Seahawks clear favorites. Can the Bears keep rising? Mike Sando 60
summary:
Matthew Stafford's Rams spent the offseason loading up after falling to the Seahawks in the NFC Championship Game. (Simon Bruty / Sports Illustrated via Getty Images)
With the NFL preseason finished, it’s time to check in with team executives to set expectations for the coming 2026 season one final time.
The six executives polled this week ranked teams 1-16 in each conference, under the condition of anonymity to allow them to speak freely. I also asked them to place each team into four buckets:
full_text:
Matthew Stafford's Rams spent the offseason loading up after falling to the Seahawks in the NFC Championship Game. (Simon Bruty / Sports Illustrated via Getty Images)
With the NFL preseason finished, it’s time to check in with team executives to set expectations for the coming 2026 season one final time.
The six executives polled this week ranked teams 1-16 in each conference, under the condition of anonymity to allow them to speak freely. I also asked them to place each team into four buckets: Super Bowl contenders, division contenders, sub-.500 teams and likely top-10 pickers in the 2027 draft.
We start with the NFC, where the Seattle Seahawks are reigning champs, but the Los Angeles Rams are the strong betting favorite. One of the execs had the Chicago Bears atop his ballot, on the thinking that seasons rarely play out as expected. Teams are ranked below in median order, with average as a tiebreaker.
Votes: 2-1-1-1-1-2 | Avg: 1.3 | Median: 1 | Vegas wins: 11.5 (1st-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 6
All but two voters moved the Rams to the top of the NFC after an offseason that saw Los Angeles overhaul its defense with Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald and two cornerbacks from Kansas City.
"I think they are the best team in the NFC by far," a former GM said. "Beyond all the defensive additions, Matthew Stafford is just surgical. So impressive."
The Rams went 1-2 against Seattle last season largely because they finished those games with a -26.7 EPA differential on special teams.
"It is hard for me to go against Seattle being the top team in the NFC," the voter putting the Seahawks atop the conference said. "Talent-wise, it is going to be really close."
One other voter had the Bears first, partly on the theory that things tend to play out unexpectedly.
"I would say there is a clear gap (between the Rams and the rest of the NFC) with the return of Aaron Donald," another voter said.
The Rams are the strongest preseason Super Bowl favorite since 2002, per covers.com.
"I think Myles Garrett puts them over the top," another exec said.
Votes: 1-2-3-2-2-6 | Avg: 2.7 | Median: 2 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 5 | Division contender: 1
The Seahawks have an unproven offensive coordinator (Brian Fleury) after Klint Kubiak's departure to become the Raiders' coach. They spent their offseason extending key players (Leonard Williams, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Devon Witherspoon) while the Rams were adding big names from the outside. The cornerback situation remains a worry, and it's unclear whether their top defensive chess piece, Nick Emmanwori, will be at his best physically following ankle surgery.
"It's hard for me to see them continuing to get better now that they are a marked man," one exec said. "A lot of people got paid. Is the hunger still there?"
The transition from hunter to hunted affects every Super Bowl winner.
"I don't know about Super Bowl, but they are going to go deep in the playoffs," another exec said. "I think them and the Packers are probably the next (NFC) teams after L.A."
Voters trust Seattle's defense while taking a wait-and-see approach with the offense.
"It is hard for me to think you're not going to have some kind of dropoff going from Kubiak to Fleury, even if it is in the same schematic realm," one voter said. "You lost Kubiak, you lost the Super Bowl MVP (Kenneth Walker III). I know you're excited about Jadarian Price, but …"
Votes: 3-4-5-3-3-4 | Avg: 3.7 | Median: 3.5 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 4 | Division contender: 2
With Seattle on "Hard Knocks" and the Rams making splash after splash this offseason, the Eagles are about as under the radar as can be. Reminder: Philly leads the league in regular-season victories over the past four seasons (50) while ranking second to Kansas City in postseason wins (six).
"They could go either way, to be quite honest," one exec said of the Eagles, who finished 11-6 last season. "I think they will be better. The thing that was really good for them is a potential concern, and that is the receiver position and running back. Saquon (Barkley) did not have a great year. The offensive line health and age is a concern. They will still be formidable."
Will A.J. Brown's departure be addition by subtraction? One voter said the pressure's on quarterback Jalen Hurts, whose relationship with Brown had grown cold and who will be playing in an overhauled offensive system under new coordinator Sean Mannion.
"It was hard for me to ding Philly even if the offense is unknown, even if they are taking a step back without A.J. Brown," another exec said. "Vic Fangio and that defense is going to be top five. That O-line is going to be pretty good. It is still Saquon Barkley. Could they win 16-13 every week? Probably."
Votes: 5-8-2-4-4-3 | Avg: 4.3 | Median: 4 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-6th-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 3 | Division contender: 3
All agree the Cowboys' offense appears formidable. How much can the defense improve?
"Anything is better than what they did last year on defense," the voter placing Dallas second in the NFC said. "They shocked the system by trading Micah Parsons, and I just think generally speaking, new coordinators on defense create variance."
No team is seeking greater variance on defense from last season than the Cowboys, who ranked 32 nd in EPA per play by a wide margin, per TruMedia. They replaced Matt Eberflus with first-time coordinator Christian Parker.
"Quinnen Williams is good, and they have a little more girth up front, so it should be better, but they've got some unknowns there too with coaches and philosophy," the voter ranking Dallas eighth said.
The voter ranking Dallas fifth thought the Cowboys' defense might outrank the Packers' defense, notable in light of the Parsons trade last year.
"I like the coordinator," this voter said of Parker. "He is going to help maximize what they have. The secondary is still not a strength, but they have an impressive front seven."
Linebacker DeMarvion Overshown's health is a key variable multiple voters highlighted.
"I have defensive concerns, for sure," one said. "Do they have enough pass rush? How healthy is Overshown? How good are the corners? But they did address the interior with Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark, and I like Caleb Downs. They will be better up the middle."
Votes: 4-7-6-7-5-1 | Avg: 5.0 | Median: 5.5 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-6th-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 2 | Division contender: 4
The one voter ranking Chicago atop the NFC said the Bears have an elite coach in Ben Johnson, a rising, super-talented quarterback in Caleb Williams and enough talent to take another step.
"I know all the regression stuff," this voter said, alluding to the Bears' ability to win seven games last season after trailing in the final two minutes. "The coach is really good, they have a really good ascending quarterback, the roster is super talented. They did all the right things in the offseason to fight the regression."
The top three teams in the NFC North are tightly bunched in these rankings.
"I love the whole NFC North," one voter said, "but the top three all have defensive concerns."
New safety Coby Bryant's season-ending knee injury hurts Chicago. The Bears still have uncertainty at left tackle.
"Can they win a playoff game again?" an exec asked. "Sure, but I guess that's where I cap the Super Bowl contender of like, do I see them coming out of the NFC over the Rams? I can't see it. Kyle (Shanahan), (Brock) Purdy and the Niners, they have been there, done that. Even Detroit, I trust."
Another voter thought the Bears' rise under Johnson last season painted a target on their backs heading into 2026.
"I'm going to double down on them," the exec placing the Bears fourth in the NFC said. "They are not going to catch people by surprise this year, and the NFC North will be tough. I still think they'll be OK."

title: How the Bengals view evolving roles at OT, WR, TE after roster reset Competition was added at swing tackle while new faces have changed the complexion of the tight end room. Paul Dehner Jr. 4
summary:

CINCINNATI – Zac Taylor last spoke into a microphone following the Bengals’ 30-13 victory against the Eagles on Friday night. Quite a bit happened over the next four days.
Thirty-five players were let go, 13 returned to the practice squad, two landed on IR-return, three joined the practice squad from other teams, one was claimed via waivers, and two players on the Bengals’ 53
full_text:
Rookie tight end Jack Endries has shown versatility during training camp and the preseason. Katie Stratman / Imagn Images
CINCINNATI – Zac Taylor last spoke into a microphone following the Bengals’ 30-13 victory against the Eagles on Friday night. Quite a bit happened over the next four days.
Thirty-five players were let go, 13 returned to the practice squad, two landed on IR-return, three joined the practice squad from other teams, one was claimed via waivers, and two players on the Bengals’ 53-man roster for 2025 opted to leave.
Kick returner was settled, competition was added at swing tackle, new faces were added at tight end, cornerback came into focus and position battles at defensive line showed their teeth.
After the first practice with the 69-man roster and practice squad on Tuesday, the Cincinnati Bengals’ early-season vision has started to come into focus.
Here’s an inside view of how the plans for three critical positions are evolving.
We must start with the glaring concern and ever-expanding competition behind Amarius Mims and Orlando Brown Jr.
Make no mistake, the swing tackle spot is still up for grabs. There are two newbies, two remaining contenders and a desperate need for somebody to step up.
The big news was that Blake Freeland was added to the practice squad from the Colts. Freeland has something nobody else in the competition can claim: An NFL regular-season snap at tackle.
Freeland was thrown in the fire as a rookie in Indianapolis, starting nine games that year, the final one coming on Christmas Eve of 2023. The 6-foot-8 Utah product lost the swing tackle job in Indianapolis the next season, then suffered a broken leg last preseason, missing the entire year. He was cleared by OTAs for the Colts, but ended up on the outside of the cut Sunday.
He’s still only 25 years old, and while he said he enjoyed his experience in Indianapolis, he is relishing the fresh start. He recognizes that time is his current advantage.
“Tackle is a game of reps,” he said. “Offensive line is a game of reps. I think it definitely helps a little bit, but we’ll see. I’m excited to work with those guys and compete with them and see where it goes.”
Meanwhile, Hinton came in after spending extra time on his first day, along with Freeland, working with offensive line coach Scott Peters.
Hinton, a 2025 sixth-round pick of the Eagles, battled in a deep room and was left on the outside behind Markel Bell and veteran Fred Johnson.
The messaging from the Bengals after they picked him up was to work on his hand technique. That just so happens to be Peters’ specialty.
“The O-line coach here, he’s amazing with it,” Hinton said. “Even just today, I’ve learned so many things about hand carriage and hand punch and location of punch, when to punch. It’s been amazing.”
Rivers will stay in the mix, but his responsibilities have grown at guard with rookie Brian Parker II now on IR-return and the other two interior line backups having no college or pro experience playing guard. Jacob Bayer just started working at guard in recent weeks.
That leaves Foster, the closest thing to an answer at swing tackle in-house this camp, as the other contender.
The biggest battle of camp now hits a second stage. The scout team reps will be critical in judging who looks like the best option for the opener and beyond.
“We’re still competing there,” Taylor said. “Guys have shown reasons why they should do it. But I won’t stand here and say this is exactly how it’s going to unfold for us. I can let them compete every week for the rest of the season. Sometimes, when you know, you know. ‘OK, this guy has just really been consistent for us and there’s no conversation about this.’ But I think right now, let’s just keep taking it with every practice we’ve got and if guys show that they’ve gotten up to speed and can do it, I’m all for however it shakes out.”
Two years ago, wide receiver Dohnte Meyers was on a practice squad for the Saskatchewan Roughriders after landing a spot on the team during an open tryout he paid $100 to attend.
Tuesday, he stood in front of a throng of media with his locker directly next to Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins.
“It’s a nice place to be,” Meyers said, looking up at the locker nameplates. “I’ve got my boys next to me. It’s gonna be a nice year.”
It’s already been pretty incredible. The story of the preseason in Cincinnati quickly went from Meyers turning heads to him carving out a real game-day role. When he got the emotional call from receivers coach Troy Walters that he made the team, the conversation quickly turned to this only being the beginning.
"This is just the beginning." pic.twitter.com/2q0j92paQM
— Cincinnati Bengals (@Bengals) August 30, 2026
Now, the Bengals are working to find the best ways to use him.
“He has earned his way — that is for sure,” Taylor said. “He just continued to make plays over and over again. We weren’t dialing stuff up for him. That is how you make it, really. When the opportunity comes your way, you have to make the most of it. We will continue to see where we can utilize him in the return game. We will continue to see where we can utilize him as a receiver. It is a tough lineup to crack. He has shown with the ball in his hands, he can be really good. He can create separation and he has a good feel.”
Meyers will enjoy extra reps during practices this week because Ja’Marr Chase (knee) and Tee Higgins (heel contusion) are both limited. There was no concern about their season status from Taylor.
“(Tee) and Ja’Marr will be good at the end of the week,” Taylor said.
Then, there’s kick returner Ke’Shawn Williams, who won the job against Charlie Jones, who landed on the New York Giants’ practice squad Tuesday.
Williams was plucked off waivers midseason last year and left enough of an impression to boot Jones off after three seasons — each of which included a return for a touchdown.
“That goes back to last season, the faith,” Taylor said. “I saw him do it live in games. So he did a great job there, made some plays as a receiver this training camp, and I just think he is a valuable weapon to have, however it shakes out, whatever his role ends up being for us on game day. He earned the opportunity, so it was good to keep him out there.”
The depth at tight end looks much different today than it did when last season concluded. In the Week 18 loss to Cleveland, Noah Fant, Cam Grandy and Tanner Hudson were all on the roster behind Drew Sample and Mike Gesicki.
Now Fant (Saints) and Grandy (Vikings PS) are gone and Hudson reverted to the practice squad on Tuesday.
Erick All and seventh-round pick Jack Endries now fill that space.
As for All, his role will not be limited in any way when the season kicks off, which Taylor confirmed on Tuesday. But Endries is here – and Grandy is not – because of a surprise last month.
“We drafted Jack because of his pass-game value, and he made the team because of what he’s done in the run game,” Taylor said. “And I’m not saying he’s there yet. He’s still got a ways to go. But that’s what I’m pleased (about). I know over time where we’ll get Jack in the pass game. I know that. It’s shown up on the tape. I know it’s there. What you don’t know when you get a tight end is how he’s going to fare in the run game and protections. And I saw the willingness, the toughness, the scrappiness to put his face in there and do that. That’s really good to see, because the more of those guys you can have, the better.”
The Bengals have utilized a tight end room with distinctly different skill sets in recent years, where Gesicki and Hudson were on the field for 80 percent of pass plays and Sample and Grandy were more indicative of run plays. They’ve looked for more All-types that are true dual threats.
The irony is they found it in the seventh round on what was projected as a pass-first type.
“You have to have a willingness to block, that’s A1, whether that’s an F-role or Y-role, he’s shown he’s more than willing to get in the mix,”…

title: Browns’ history suggests Shedeur Sanders will eventually get his chance this season Cleveland has had at least three different starting quarterbacks in each of the last three seasons. Zac Jackson 12
summary:

The Cleveland Browns are shifting out of preseason mode and beginning to prepare their remade offense for the Week 1 opener in Jacksonville.
In late August, new coach Todd Monken announced that Deshaun Watson would be the team’s starting quarterback after an offseason competition with Shedeur Sanders. With Watson having not play
full_text:
Shedeur Sanders, who started seven games for the Browns last season, was beat out by Deshaun Watson in a QB competition during training camp. Jason Miller / Getty Images
The Cleveland Browns are shifting out of preseason mode and beginning to prepare their remade offense for the Week 1 opener in Jacksonville.
In late August, new coach Todd Monken announced that Deshaun Watson would be the team’s starting quarterback after an offseason competition with Shedeur Sanders. With Watson having not played since 2024 and being signed only for this season, the team’s future depth chart at quarterback appears completely open — and the path seemed clear for Cleveland to keep four passers on its active roster.
The Browns did keep four in the building, but not on their initial 53-man roster , as Dillon Gabriel was placed on injured reserve with a designation to return after the season’s first four games.
Gabriel isn’t eligible to participate in practice until October, so Monken said Sanders and rookie Taylen Green will split the scout-team reps as the Browns begin working on Jacksonville’s schemes and tendencies.
Though nothing was guaranteed given that Green was clearly fourth in line through the summer and the team’s plans for the rookie seemed to trend more toward preparing him to play in 2027 than 2026, Green was always likely to make the regular-season roster but wasn’t a lock.
And though the Browns might eventually use Green’s athleticism in short-yardage or special packages, the focus for now will be on him continuing to develop, maximizing his scout-team reps and preparing to be the emergency game day quarterback.
Sanders is next in line. That doesn’t necessarily mean first-team practice reps like he got almost every other day through the spring and summer, but this Browns coaching staff views Sanders like the last one did: as a developmental quarterback with enough tools to eventually become a full-time player.
Sanders spent six weeks as Cleveland’s primary backup last season before starting the final seven games. But he never got practice reps with the No. 1 offense before he was pressed into game action. He’s now had an entire offseason to learn Monken’s scheme and work with various offensive personnel groups, so he should be more ready when called upon.
History says that’s more of a “when” than an “if.” The Browns have had at least three different starting quarterbacks in each of the last three seasons — and 12 times since the team returned to the NFL in 1999. The primary backup to begin the season has started at least one pre-November game for Cleveland in seven of the last 10 years.
Watson has played just 19 games over four seasons for the Browns. And should the season go south at some point, they would likely want to evaluate Sanders, who’s signed for three more years.
So while nothing is guaranteed, Sanders will be one play away from having his number called, and will have upcoming practice weeks to continue showing Monken he’s game-ready.
“I thought Shedeur did a lot of really good things (this summer),” Monken said. “I’m really proud of him and how far he’s come from the moment I got here to now. Very impressive.
“He plays with a lot of confidence … we look forward to Shedeur continuing to grow as a player.”
As part of announcing his starting quarterback decision, Monken acknowledged that he always valued Watson’s seven previous seasons of NFL experience because the Browns will have almost a totally new offensive huddle when they play their first two games on the road.
In following hints he’d dropped earlier in training camp, Monken also said he long viewed Watson as being ahead from an operational standpoint and that Sanders was “making up ground” in those areas.
“You see quarterbacks go in there and right away play well, and you’ve seen others that need some time,” Monken said. “(For) some, it happens quicker than others, and some have further to go. … From the jump in the offseason, when (Sanders) showed some things that I really liked and (showed) the way he’s wired, that’s when we made the decision to give him more reps. That’s when we decided to make it a competition for Shedeur, and for us.
“That was the point of it all, to get where he’s at today. Because early on, in my opinion, it was pretty obvious that Deshaun was ahead — his experience, right? He should be. We made that decision, and where (Sanders is) today is a byproduct of that. I’m excited about the long game for him. There are certain things he has to continue to work on, and he’s going to continue to grow leaps and bounds because he’s a sponge. He takes it all in, he really does. So, I just think it’s a matter of time before we get a chance to see that.”
Green ran a 40-yard dash in 4.36 seconds at the NFL Scouting Combine in February. He waited until the sixth round of April’s draft to hear his name called because he’s more of a runner than a passer at this point.
Green got no competitive full-team reps in the spring and only a handful over the first three weeks of training camp. Monken has called Green “smart as heck” and said the only way a quarterback in his spot could make the roster would be by mastering the playbook and staying ready for the minimal live reps he received.
After Green threw a touchdown pass and then ran for another in a short stint in the Aug. 20 joint practice with the Buffalo Bills , he saw his first preseason action in the second half versus New England last week.
Mostly, though, Green spent his summer participating in meetings and individual drills. During full-team drills, he was mostly a spectator, often lining up behind the participating quarterback and walking himself through the plays.
Green showed off his speed in that game, and now each week in practice he’ll try to show his coaches he’s improving as a passer in his scout-team opportunities.
“Now I just continue to do what I’ve been doing,” Green said. “I didn’t get a lot in training camp, but I still got some mental reps and (would) just be behind Deshaun or Shedeur. I just continue to ask questions.
“I’m in a great quarterback room, and those guys have a lot of knowledge. So I continue to ask questions there, and I keep asking my coaches questions.”

title: The NFL’s 10 worst quarterback situations: How does the Browns' disaster compare? Saad Yousuf 97
summary:
The Browns start the year with Deshaun Watson, right, as the starter and second-year QB Shedeur Sanders, left, as his backup. Nick Cammett / Getty Images
In the time of year when hope generally springs eternal, teams that enter the regular season with confidence in their quarterback situation feel better about their chances for a successful season.

full_text:
The Browns start the year with Deshaun Watson, right, as the starter and second-year QB Shedeur Sanders, left, as his backup. Nick Cammett / Getty Images
In the time of year when hope generally springs eternal, teams that enter the regular season with confidence in their quarterback situation feel better about their chances for a successful season.
The most important part of the quarterback discussion revolves around the starter. However, the full depth chart matters. Since 2022, there hasn’t been a season in which more than half of the teams in the league didn’t turn to somebody other than their starter for at least two games. Several factors come into play, including performance-based benchings and resting starters toward the end of the season. But injuries play a major role, too.
As we did last year, let’s examine the 10 worst quarterback situations in the NFL entering the 2026 season. As a reminder, this considers each team’s full depth chart. It is not simply a ranking of starting quarterbacks, although the starting situation will weigh more heavily, and the backups will be weighed relative to other backups across the league.
This season, we are using The Athletic’s QB Tiers as a source of guidance. There were 17 quarterbacks that fell into the Tier 1 or Tier 2 category. The weight of having a starter at that level kept those teams above this particular discussion. Last year, teams with rookie starting quarterbacks were exempt from this exercise but this year, there are no teams entering the season with a rookie slated to be the starter.
Starter (QB Tier ranking): Bryce Young (Tier 3, No. 22)
Backups: Kenny Pickett, Haynes King
Young is one of the more frustrating quarterbacks in the NFL. He’ll put forth enough bad performances to show that he’s not the answer the franchise thought he would be when they traded up to draft him No. 1. However, just when you start cementing that opinion, he’ll have a game or two that pulls you back in. This season should go a long way toward giving the Panthers some clarity on if Young deserves a second contract.
Pickett is a comfortable backup for Carolina, in that he could be serviceable in the short term, but his presence also won’t make Young, who has already gone through an unceremonious benching, nervous about his job.
Starter (QB Tier ranking): Kyler Murray (Tier 3, No. 23)
Backups: J.J. McCarthy, Carson Wentz
Murray’s recent history on the field doesn’t inspire much confidence, but with the way things are run in Arizona, it’s fair to wonder if the change in scenery will unlock Murray’s full potential. Playing in Kevin O’Connell’s system and with a supporting cast featuring Justin Jefferson, Jauan Jennings and Jordan Addison should help, too. Murray is squarely in the middle of Tier 3, but his upside could take him to the top of that tier.
Minnesota’s backup situation is fairly deep. McCarthy is fine as a No. 2 and last year’s No. 2 for the Vikings, Carson Wentz, profiles as one of the better No. 3 quarterbacks in the league. If Wentz ends up being the No. 2, either because McCarthy is no longer on the roster or even over McCarthy, the floor of Minnesota’s offense should remain solid.
Starter (QB Tier ranking): Cam Ward (Tier 3, No. 25)
Ward is a tough evaluation because the Titans were so depleted offensively last year in his rookie season. Not only was the talent on the roster lacking, but Ward also dealt with a change in play-calling duties three weeks into 2025 and the firing of the head coach who drafted him four weeks later. Changes on the coaching staff and adding the likes of Wan’Dale Robinson and Carnell Tate should help.
Having a veteran backup in Trubisky, who has 58 NFL starts under his belt, is an upgrade over what Tennessee had last season. Trubisky should be able to step in and handle short stints, if needed.
Starter (QB Tier ranking): Daniel Jones (Tier 3, No. 21)
Backups: Riley Leonard, Anthony Richardson Sr.
This position largely depends on how Daniel Jones is viewed, both from an on-field play perspective and from a medical standpoint. Jones has had a largely subpar NFL career but he found a style of play through the first half of last season that allowed the Colts to win games. Jones may not be viewed as a quarterback who can carry a team to wins, but if he can at least not be a reason they lose, he’ll be doing his part. A big part of the mystery with Jones also revolves around how he rebounds from last year’s mid-season Achilles injury.
Behind Jones are Leonard and Richardson, the same guys that were on the roster last year when the Colts felt they had to go pull Philip Rivers out of retirement for the home stretch. If the Colts have to ride either for long stretches, there’s nothing to suggest that the team won’t be playing for a draft slot instead of a playoff spot.
Starter (QB Tier ranking): Tyler Shough (Tier 3, No. 26)
Backups: Spencer Rattler, Zach Wilson
The Saints feel like they may have found the stability at the position they’ve been looking for in the post-Drew Brees era. Shough came off the bench last season and had some promising showings but there wasn’t the sample size necessary to anoint him as the next one. Still, quarterbacks with promising flashes typically get the benefit of the doubt until proven otherwise. Behind Shough, there’s not a whole lot of hope. Rattler has a 1-13 career record in the NFL and Wilson hasn’t started a game since 2023.
Starter (QB Tier ranking): Tua Tagovailoa (Tier 3, No. 26-tie) or Michael Penix Jr. (Tier 4, No. 32)
Backups: Cooper Rush, Jack Strand
There have been legitimate concerns swirling around Penix since he was drafted by the Falcons, just after they signed Kirk Cousins to a big free-agent contract. With his lack of durability and inefficient play, Penix hasn’t done much to silence those questions. When healthy, he should be the best option for Atlanta, but he was only recently cleared for full 11-on-11 work and the Falcons have yet to determine a starter.
As a backup, Tagovailoa should be one of the better options in the NFL, given that he’s only two years removed from being paid as one of the best starters in the league. Rush is more than serviceable as a No. 3 and the system in Atlanta is better suited for him compared to the strange fit in Baltimore last season. Strand had an impressive preseason and gives Atlanta another developmental option.
Starter (QB Tier ranking): Malik Willis (Tier 4, No. 29)
Backups: Brady Cook, Kyle McCord
If we were judging by quarterback cap sheets, the Dolphins would probably fall below every team except the Browns. Tagovailoa’s cap hit will be tough to navigate, but the Dolphins still decided to hand a relatively hefty deal to Willis in free agency. Willis has six starts in four seasons. The franchise also did him no favors by trading away Jaylen Waddle, even if it was the right thing to do.
Behind Willis, the Dolphins have one of the worst backup quarterback situations in the league. None of the three quarterbacks Miami had throughout training camp — Quinn Ewers, Cam Miller and Mark Gronowski — are on the roster anymore. Cook wasn’t even able to stick on the New York Jets roster, despite their lackluster quarterback situation (though it would be foolish to draw conclusions about a quarterback based on how the Jets felt about him). McCord entered the league as an undrafted free agent last year and is an unknown commodity with no NFL experience.
Starter (QB Tier ranking): Jacoby Brissett (Tier 4, No. 33)
Backups: Gardner Minshew, Carson Beck
If you’re in a situation where you not only have Brissett holding out over a contract dispute but, as a team, you decide to give in to his demands, things are not going well. In fairness to Arizona, it didn’t appear the Cardinals had any intention of fielding high-level quarterback play this season. They seem content spending the 2026 season recovering from the Kyler Murray era after releasing him this offseason and turning their hopes for an answer at the…

full_text:
Jonah Elliss and Que Robinson should see expanded roles this season. Bart Young / Associated Press
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — Que Robinson used a speedy dip-and-dash move to create space against the offensive tackle and then bury Packers quarterback Kyle McCord for a sack in the Broncos’ second exhibition game earlier this month.
It may have been his first takedown of this preseason, Denver’s second-year pass rusher explained afterward, but it was hardly an unfamiliar outcome.
“Shoot, man, I’ve been giving our offensive tackles hell all camp,” Robinson said with a grin, “so it feels pretty good to go against someone else and work a move that I’ve been practicing for I don’t know how long. It felt pretty good.”
Robinson produced an 18.4 percent pressure rate in the preseason, ranking fourth out of 169 players credited with at least 35 defensive pass-rush snaps, according to TruMedia. He had four quarterback hits, routinely moving passers off their marks as he waved his rangy arms in pursuit. When the Broncos open the regular season on Sept. 14 at Kansas City, they are expecting more of the same from a young player who has suddenly been thrust into a far more substantial role.
Starting outside linebacker Jonathon Cooper on Sunday was placed on the NFL’s commissioner exempt list as the league continues investigating the circumstances surrounding two of June arrests, making him ineligible to play in games or practice with the team. It’s not clear when Cooper will be removed from the list or whether he’ll face a suspension after the league’s investigation is complete. The 28-year-old pleaded not guilty to all five charges stemming from a pair of domestic incidents with his then-girlfriend during an arraignment hearing in a Douglas County (Colo.) courtroom Monday afternoon. A trial in the case is scheduled to begin Nov. 10.
The Broncos are operating on the assumption that they won’t have Cooper in the lineup. The silver lining is that defensive coordinator Vance Joseph will be able to achieve the goals he established early in the season — finding more time on the field for Robinson and third-year edge rusher Jonah Elliss, who will likely get the first crack at replacing Cooper in the starting lineup. There was an idea within Denver’s coaching staff at the start of the offseason that Elliss could switch to inside linebacker with veterans Alex Singleton and Justin Strnad set to enter free agency — both ultimately re-signed with the Broncos. The conversation, though, Joseph said, was really about finding more ways for Elliss to be on the field. The 2024 third-round pick out of Utah played 38 percent of Denver’s defensive snaps in each of his first two seasons.
“My take on Jonah is, when you watched our cut-ups after the season, he played really well, but he didn’t play enough. Same with Que,” Joseph said during the second week of training camp, before Cooper had been placed on the exempt list. “So to get (Elliss) on the field more often and maybe packaged (at inside linebacker) so we can play Que more often also, it’s really team-based to get our better players more reps. If he’s one of our better players, I don’t want him to be watching. I want him to be playing.”
Robinson has been patiently waiting for this opportunity ever since he arrived at Alabama. He played his first two seasons behind Will Anderson (first-round pick in 2023) and another year behind Dallas Turner (first-rounder in 2024). With more playing time as a senior in 2024, Robinson had four sacks and showed enough flashes on the edge — and on special teams — for the Broncos to spend a fourth-round pick and add to an already strong outside linebacker group. That depth made Robinson an inactive player on game day 11 out of 17 weeks during his rookie season, but he insists he didn’t struggle to be patient. Not with all there was to learn from a group in front of him — Cooper, Elliss, Nik Bonitto and Dondrea Tillman — that was helping Joseph’s defense set a franchise sack record for the second season in a row.
“I sat by these guys and being able to watch them get to like 68 sacks and stuff like and, man, you get to see the technicality side of it,” Robinson said midway through what became a breakout training camp. “Why they made a certain move and when did they make it? How did they time it up? I just took it all in and just now I’m just getting a chance to apply it.”
Robinson got to apply it on the biggest stage of his young career when he was active for the Broncos in the AFC Championship Game. He was lined up on the left edge on a second-and-6 for the Patriots late in the first quarter. Robinson read a bootleg immediately at the snap and shoved the flat receiver, tight end Hunter Henry, off his mark, disrupting the primary read for quarterback Drake Maye. Before the quarterback could adjust, Robinson zoomed into the backfield and dragged Maye down by the shoulder pads.
“It’s a lot easier when you’ve got older guys who believe in you,” said Robinson, who has worked on a side field at the Broncos’ practices this week but did so in full pads Tuesday.
“… It was a good thing for me to hear that from them, especially being in my sixth game, not really thinking I’d be playing in that game. It was a good feeling just to know my teammates were behind me. It gave me confidence to go make those kind of plays.”
Broncos general manager George Paton referenced Robinson’s appearance in that conference title game — and scores of big games Elliss has played in the past two years — as he voiced confidence that Denver’s defense can withstand Cooper’s absence, however long it lingers. There is no brushing aside the impact the veteran has made while registering 27 sacks across his last three seasons as a full-time starter, while also being a stout edge-setter in the run game.
The Broncos, though, have been eager to get their young pass rushers on the field more frequently. That time is now.

full_text:
Danielle Hunter and Will Anderson Jr. return to the front lines of Houston's elite defense. Alex Slitz / Getty Images
After three consecutive trips to the divisional round, the Houston Texans have established themselves as contenders. The team went 12-5 last season and entered the playoffs riding nine consecutive wins. A 30-6 wild-card victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers delivered the franchise’s first road playoff win, before a five-turnover loss against the New England Patriots ended any hopes of Houston’s first AFC title game appearance.
DeMeco Ryans heads into his fourth season as head coach, with Matt Burke back as defensive coordinator. Houston’s nasty defense stays mostly intact, highlighted by the likes of Will Anderson Jr., Danielle Hunter, Derek Stingley Jr. and Kamari Lassiter. Last year, the relentless unit boasted top-three rankings in points allowed, yards allowed and takeaways.
But to take the next step, the Texans need more from their offense. Houston made several offseason moves designed to retool the offense. The team traded for running back David Montgomery and receiver Kayshon Boutte, and signed veteran linemen Braden Smith and Wyatt Teller. Its most important pieces remain in place, though. C.J. Stroud returns in a critical year for the quarterback, Nico Collins is still his top target and Tank Dell is working his way back from the catastrophic knee injury that cost him the entire 2025 season.
The schedule offers plenty of national exposure: Houston has four primetime games in the back half of the schedule, most notably a Christmas Eve showdown with the Philadelphia Eagles. The Texans also have Week 6 trip to Wembley Stadium to face the Jacksonville Jaguars.
Be sure to follow the Texans on The Athletic . Scoop City delivers updates from around the NFL, “ The Athletic Football Show ” breaks down the league in depth, and the national staff covers everything from power rankings and fantasy football to injuries, transactions and feature reporting.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC and is currently scheduled to carry eight Houston games. The network’s theme music is also a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars Texans legend JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The Texans play in the final Monday night game of the regular season when they visit the Green Bay Packers in Week 17; it airs on ESPN only. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Houston has two Thursday night games: at home against the Indianapolis Colts in Week 11, and on the road in Philadelphia on Christmas Eve.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung…

full_text:
The Jaguars will face challenges no other team in the NFL will encounter. Coach Liam Coen has been preparing to overcome them since the spring. Rich Storry / Getty Images
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. — The reminders of the construction are everywhere: an echoing thud in the middle of a meeting, reverberating ripples dancing atop a cup of coffee, the drills humming somewhere off in the distance.
EverBank Stadium, home of the Jacksonville Jaguars, is very much an active construction site, and the football team can’t exactly tune out the noise — not with the auxiliary parking lots and giant cranes that meet them in the morning or with the subtle jolts scattered throughout the day. And to be perfectly fair, a $1.4 billion “Stadium of the Future” renovation can’t really be limited to banker’s hours if it’s going to be ready for 2028.
Jaguars head coach Liam Coen immediately recognized the potential for excuses, for those temporary distractions to slowly erode the team’s focus. So he flipped it as the Jags reported for training camp and generated a new source of motivation.
“I wanted to get out ahead of that,” Coen told The Athletic . “I said, ‘Guys, we’re going to hear this. We’re going to see it. We may feel it. But it ain’t gonna be a f—ing reason. It’s not going to be an excuse. Because at the end of the day, nobody cares in this league. Nobody cares.’”
The Jaguars play six games this season at EverBank Stadium, conceding important home games against the Philadelphia Eagles and Houston Texans to venues in London ; the Jaguars will travel to Camping World Stadium in Orlando for all home games in 2027. They’ll play 28 of their next 34 regular-season games outside of Jacksonville.
Coen was on vacation this summer with Jaguars general manager James Gladstone and executive vice president of football operations Tony Boselli when he decided to be proactive about tackling any potential construction complaints with the team.
And so the mindset was born: Anytime. Anywhere. Any place.
The Jacksonville Globetrotters will invite the competition however it comes. Because if they’re going to build off a 13-4 record in Coen’s first season, they must face the reality that the standings shed no emotion, and there’s no selection committee to save them.
“You’re going to hear that a lot as an excuse, as a reason, as a whatever,” Coen said. “Our whole mindset is, ‘Anytime, anywhere, any place.’ Doesn’t matter. That’s what we’re training every day. That’s the culture piece, trying to show them how we have the mindset and mentality every time we walk into this building, that it doesn’t matter where we are, doesn’t matter what time it is, doesn’t matter who we’re playing, where we’re playing. You’re going to get the best version of me every day.”
Coen leaned on his coaching peers this offseason while researching the challenges he’d encounter as a second-year coach. The organization has also gone through recent struggles with second-year coaches, going 3-13 in 2014 with Gus Bradley, 5-11 in 2018 (after reaching the AFC Championship Game a season before) with Doug Marrone and falling out of the playoffs despite staying level at 9-8 in 2023 with Doug Pederson.
To build off the greatest turnaround ever by a rookie coach, Coen learned that he could not sacrifice team culture. Coen, those around the team have said, established an incredibly welcoming atmosphere in 2025, and his ability to create a positive culture has been a strength.
But he couldn’t take it for granted.
So, when the Jaguars face adversity, whether it’s a built-in scheduling quirk or a taxing loss, Coen said, they have to be able to lean on their commitment to one another. They’ll all be judged on their record.
“It’s a results-based business, but that’s why we have to lean into our process now more than ever,” Coen said. “The process drives those results, not living in the result. And when the schedule came out, I heard, ‘You’re playing Houston in London, so you’re basically playing Houston twice away.’ Nobody cares, though. At the end of the day, when our season is done, nobody is going to have an asterisk there, so we can’t even let our minds go there. That cannot be a reason, an excuse, a single thought.
“Put us in a helicopter, fly us out into the frigging desert and let’s go play. That’s the mindset we’re training every single day.”
It started in the spring. Across the board, Jaguars players reported in April for voluntary workouts, still fuming over the home playoff loss to the Buffalo Bills. But they’ve used that as fuel for the upcoming season, recognizing their progress while aiming to push or even shatter their limits.
“When you get in,” Coen said, “everybody had a similar mindset of, ‘How good can we be? … It’s like, ‘Guys, we have not arrived. We had a good year, and we know we have a chance. But there’s a whole other level we’ve got to get to.’”
To sharpen their intentionality throughout the offseason workout program, Coen borrowed a “three better, three best” project from his time on Sean McVay’s staff with the Los Angeles Rams. Coen’s Jags staff put together individual development plans for each player, including three of their best qualities the team should continue to emphasize and three qualities that require refinement.
Coen devoted the first week of OTAs to the project, meeting with each player to discuss their “three better, three best” outline and the accompanying film cutups that drove home each point. They were specific points, too, such as pace to the line of scrimmage, improving eye discipline in zone coverage for a linebacker and learning new stance techniques for offensive linemen, among hundreds of examples. They geared time on the field, virtual and team meeting rooms to those coaching points in search of tangible results.
“That’s what we attacked all spring,” Coen said. “Our guys did a nice job with it.”
Coen tapped into a bit more creativity for the final week of the spring, conducting a three-day passing camp with a host of NFL alumni including DeMarcus Ware, Fred Taylor, Maurice Jones-Drew, Devin and Jason McCourty, Marcedes Lewis, Ben Watson, Corey Linsley and Alejandro Villanueva.
Despite being a voluntary stretch on the heels of mandatory minicamp, Coen said they had “damn-near 100 percent attendance.” Aside from fieldwork, they had banquet-style dinners for the former players to share their stories and lend advice.
“It was awesome,” Coen said. “Anything those guys could provide is going to help make us better. What can’t DeMarcus Ware tell Travon Walker, Josh Hines-Allen, Arik Armstead to give them an edge? I mean, I got better as a coach from the McCourty twins being here, no doubt.”
Coen’s father was a longtime coach, and his late mother was a teacher, so he’s got a natural ability at finding creative ways to command a room. His locker room celebrations went viral through the Jaguars’ social media accounts, as the 40-year-old’s excitement and authenticity shone.
Those were just peeks into his day-to-day work throughout the season, but Coen is also brutally realistic about two things. First, the messages will grow stale if they aren’t winning. And second, the team’s buy-in wouldn’t be nearly as strong if they didn’t believe in him, too.
“When the players know you’re honest with them, you’re going to hold yourself accountable as a coach; you’re going to hold the people around you to a standard,” Coen said. “If you screw up as a coach, we can be honest about that: ‘I didn’t put you in the best position to be successful.’ I think that’s when things can get dark when it’s bad. I say, ‘Guys, it’s OK to say we screwed up because now we can move on. Now we can go fix it and improve.’ But if nobody is willing to step up and say it, we’re going to have some problems, and that goes from the top down.”
Whether it’s coaches, players, video coordinators or anyone else, there’s a welcomed environment of accountability. Coen mentioned a couple of video assistants who popped into his office to…
