Cyrus Allen has been one of the Chiefs' stars of the summer, but rookie wide receivers typically need time to get fully comfortable with Andy Reid's playbook. Jay Biggerstaff / Imagn Images
Kansas City Chiefs coach Andy Reid is ready to tell a training camp story.
It’s two weeks ago in his office dorm room at Missouri Western, and in a short anecdote, Reid is about to reveal exactly where the Chiefs stand when it comes to the potential of fifth-round receiver Cyrus Allen.
While also speaking about some of the expected pitfalls the rookie could face.
Reid said it was evident then that Allen was still getting all the play calls down. During practices — and also the first preseason game against the Los Angeles Rams — he wasn’t always ending up where he was supposed to.
What happened immediately after, though, Reid says, is just important.
“Even when there were a couple routes he ran the wrong thing and lined up the wrong way in the game, the quarterback still threw the ball to him. He made the catch,” Reid said with a smile. “You go, ‘All right. There’s a certain trust there.’ And he’ll work through all the other stuff.”
This is where the complexity lies with Allen — and also in trying to predict his rookie season, even after he was one of the team’s top performers during August’s practices.
The flashes have been there. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes labeled Allen as one of the team’s standouts at the end of training camp, and the fact that he kept peppering him with the ball while covered in the summer’s organized team activities signaled that the young receiver has already built up chemistry with his QB.
There’s a reason, though, that rookie receivers typically need time to become fully comfortable with Reid’s extensive playbook.
After the team’s second preseason game against Tampa Bay, Allen acknowledged in the locker room that recalling information remains an obstacle as he trains at all three receiver positions.
“Just slowing down my thought process,” Allen said when describing what he was working on most, “and just having to learn everything.”
Zoom out to the bigger picture — while projecting not just this season but the next four — and it’s easy to see why the Chiefs have been so encouraged by Allen.
Reid is quick to say he’s “got tools in there that work in this offense.” Receiver teammate Xavier Worthy has called Allen an “electric route runner,” while assistant general manager Mike Bradway says he takes coaching well with a unique skill set.
“We try to temper expectations a little bit, but you can just be out here watching him move around,” Bradway told The Athletic at training camp on Aug. 19. “You can tell he belongs.”
Allen’s path to Kansas City — and the NFL — wasn’t always direct. He wasn’t invited to the NFL combine, which meant teams had to do extra work to figure out if he was worth adding as a late-round draft pick.
Through it all, Allen said the Chiefs remained one of the most interested teams in him from the start.
It meant something a few months ago — and still does now.
“I appreciate that, for them having me here,” Allen said. “So I’ve got to make them right.”
Immediately after his pro day at Cincinnati in late March, Allen was on the road to Kansas City.
The Chiefs scheduled him for his first top-30 visit. And Allen said the timing wasn’t a coincidence.
“They were honest with me,” Allen said. “They were like, ‘You’re a dawg. We wanted you here. That’s why we got you up here early.'”
Chiefs vice president of player personnel Ryne Nutt said in April that Allen’s impressive run through the all-star game circuit demanded the team take an extended look.
Allen first stood out at the American Bowl, with Nutt saying he was “routing up dudes left and right” while displaying quickness and elite route-running ability. After that, Allen was just as impressive against better competition in the Senior Bowl, which moved him further up the Chiefs’ board.
“Throughout the process,” Nutt said, “we just felt like he crushed it.”
That continued during Allen’s top-30 visit in K.C.
Bradway remembered talking with Allen in his office for about 15 minutes, with his demeanor standing out immediately.
“The kid was just a ton of juice, ton of confidence, ton of personality,” Bradway said. “He carries himself like he knows he’s a good player, and he’s used that slight at the combine for motivation.”
Chiefs northeast area scout Cassidy Kaminski, meanwhile, said in April that his chat with Allen stood out as “one of the best interviews that I had.” Allen’s tone reflected some New Orleans swagger from his hometown, yet his words also came across as both passionate and authentic.
In terms of competitive energy and bravado, Kaminski immediately flashed back to his first interactions with former Chiefs running back Isiah Pacheco — a hard-nosed player who helped set the practice tone during his four seasons with the team.
Kaminski also said Allen’s coaches at Cincinnati gave positive reviews about how he bounced back from a dislocated elbow before his senior season. Allen’s work ethic then seemed to reflect a bigger theme about who he was.
“Yeah, he’s 185 pounds,” Kaminski said, “but pound-for-pound, you’re not going to question this kid’s toughness in any capacity.”
The Chiefs had all this in mind before reshuffling their NFL Draft board on Day 3.
Bradway said a pair of skill-position players, Allen and Nebraska running back Emmett Johnson, moved toward the top of the team’s list based on their on-field traits and willingness to take coaching. Those two also had consensus buy-in across the organization among coaches, scouts and support staff, who all believed that they’d be productive with the Chiefs.
K.C. traded up to select Johnson with the 161st pick, then took Allen after that at No. 176.
Almost immediately, Bradway said he heard from colleagues outside the building about Allen.
“He’s one of those guys where you pick him, and you get a ton of texts from guys around the league saying, ‘We really liked him,'” Bradway said. “It was one of those where the process kind of pays off — where you really identify a guy months before the draft.”
While it’s too early to know how all this will end up, Allen has certainly made good on his first impression.
As early as June, Worthy was saying Allen had a “special ability to him.” Bradway also says some of the Chiefs’ scouting beliefs about Allen were reinforced during his first few months; most notably, Allen plays faster on the field than his 4.47-second 40-yard dash time would suggest, and he also shows an innate feel for how to get open against man coverage.
The Chiefs’ internal feelings about Allen also have been reflected in the moves they didn’t make. While many outsiders suggested they should add a veteran receiver as insurance, the fact they didn’t shows that they’ve seen enough from Allen not to want to block some of his expected playing time with another body.
Now, of course, comes the hard part — even if it might sound simple to most of the outside world.
Receivers coach Chad O’Shea says the biggest hurdle for Allen is getting accustomed to NFL play calls. That means getting in the huddle, processing the quarterback’s words, getting lined up correctly to the left or right side of the formation, then positioning with the exact alignment and split to ensure proper spacing with teammates.
“All those things are new, and they’re new to most players who are rookies in this league,” O’Shea said on Aug. 19. “We’ve just got to continue to really focus on those things, and great things will happen if we focus on the little things.”
It’s that hidden part of the game that has kept rookie receivers from getting early production in Reid’s offense before. And that’s not even taking into account that Allen is working to learn all of the Chiefs’ receiver positions — something the team doesn’t typically ask of its wideouts early in their rookie years.

full_text:
Stan Kroenke, left, has a portfolio of successful teams in his ownership group. Michael Regan / Getty Images For Premier League
Los Angeles Angels fans rejoiced on Tuesday after news broke that longtime owner Arte Moreno was selling the team for $4 billion to Stan Kroenke, whose Kroenke Sports and Entertainment owns a collection of franchises across multiple leagues.
Under the group’s umbrella, Kroenke owns the NFL’s Los Angeles Rams, NBA’s Denver Nuggets, NHL’s Colorado Avalanche and Arsenal in the English Premier League. He also owns MLS’ Colorado Rapids and the National Lacrosse League’s Colorado Mammoth. Each of those teams has won at least one league title during Kroenke’s ownership tenure.
So what impact will the ownership change — which is expected to become official in the first quarter of 2027, pending MLB approval — have on the Angels? We asked writers at The Athletic who have covered Kroenke’s other franchises to shed some light based on their experiences.
How would you describe KSE’s ownership style of the team you cover?
Jourdan Rodrigue (Senior NFL writer and former Rams beat writer): Kroenke’s philosophy with the Rams’ football operations is largely hands-off. While the leadership group — consisting of Kevin Demoff, Tony Pastoors, Les Snead and Sean McVay — does run major transactions by Kroenke for final approval (such as their high-profile trades for quarterback Matthew Stafford and more recently for defensive end Myles Garrett), he signs checks and lets the football experts do their jobs. It has worked to the tune of two Super Bowl appearances and one win since the Rams’ return to L.A. in 2016.
The key word is “experts.” One area where I’d expect Kroenke and Demoff, his deputy, to make an early statement is in the hiring/appointing/empowering of various coaches and executives to run the club. Historically, the ownership group has found a lot of success in pairing a younger, creative general manager with an up-and-coming coach (in the Rams’ case, Snead and McVay). Kroenke has recently followed that model with Arsenal, too.
Amy Lawrence, Arsenal beat writer: There is not a straight answer to this because one of the most important elements of the relationship between KSE and Arsenal is how it has changed over time. They may have arrived with one idea about how they intended to run the club, but that has evolved considerably in the years that followed. At the start, KSE recognised that English/European football was not their area of expertise so they took a hands-off role, and put absolute trust in the hierarchy at the club to run it well. That included Ivan Gazidis, who had once been heavily involved in strategic and business plans at MLS. To supporters of the club, the Kroenkes were initially regarded as absent owners, and that was interpreted as a lack of caring.
Two things changed quite radically. Firstly, KSE evolved from being partial investors to outright owners. Then they became much more directly involved, particularly in the case of Josh, who spent a period in London learning and observing. That led to much greater oversight and influence in the big decisions and a much closer bond, which reached a climax when Josh and his father Stan were invited to bring the Premier League trophy won by Arsenal for the first time in 22 years onto the pitch to be presented. By now, their stewardship was recognised by supporters whose tune towards their owners had been transformed by trust and success.
Peter Baugh (NHL staff writer and former Avalanche beat writer): During my time in Denver (late 2020 to late 2023), the Kroenkes seemed to give latitude to the Joe Sakic-led Avalanche front office to make the moves it deemed necessary. The NHL has a hard cap, so the Kroenkes don’t have to worry about luxury tax bills with the Avalanche like they do with some of their other teams, and they were willing to spend up to it with Colorado in a prime contention window. That’s continued since I left, and KSE was willing to give star defenseman Cale Makar the richest contract in NHL history just last week. They found a system that worked under Sakic and Chris MacFarland (the team’s assistant general manager-turned general manager who now runs the Nashville Predators) and trusted their executives. In terms of facilities, the Avalanche have a somewhat outdated practice rink that lacks the polish of some other teams in the league. And though Josh Kroenke has discussed upgrades to the Avalanche and Nuggets practice facilities, that has remained a need for both teams.
Mike Vorkunov (national basketball business reporter) : The Nuggets have had success during the Kroenke era. They are in a tie for the fifth-highest winning percentage since Stan took over in 2000. The Nuggets even won a title in 2023, which was a capstone to the ownership period. But the Nuggets have earned criticism lately for not making the most of the last few years, while Nikola Jokic, arguably the best player in the sport, has been on their team. They have shown an unwillingness to spend into the luxury tax during their ownership (six times since the start of the 2001-02 season) and in the last few years have shed key players instead of increasing payroll and living with some of the NBA’s most punitive roster-building and tax punishments. The Nuggets were also off local cable for large parts of their market for five-and-a-half years because Kroenke Sports and Entertainment, which owns their local RSN, couldn’t cut a deal with Comcast.
What have been some key elements of their tenure when it comes to acquiring players (free agency, transfer market, trades). Do they distinguish themselves from others in their league in any ways?
Rodrigue: The Rams are known for their agility. They have pivoted on multiple occasions from a draft-and-develop team-building model to what popularly became known as the “F them picks” model, where they trade high-capital draft picks for premier players at premium positions such as quarterback, cornerback or pass rusher. The team loves to invest in acquired stars, which is a tribute to their neighbors, the Lakers and Dodgers. But they’ve also been able to draft extremely well to build home-grown talent (receivers Cooper Kupp and Puka Nacua, both middle to late-round draft picks; defensive tackle Kobie Turner and, of course, recently unretired defensive tackle Aaron Donald). They also are well-regarded across the league for their innovation, whether through McVay and the rest of the coaching staff and how his scheme has informed much of the modern era of the sport, or through Snead and the front office and their counter-cultural methods for scouting and talent identification.
Lawrence: Arsenal are unusual in that they preach a pursuit of ambition while remaining self-sustaining. In a market place where they are up against nation states or not so long ago oligarchs (for example two of their biggest rivals, Manchester City and Chelsea, have been charged with financial irregularities) they are committed to playing by the rules.
Since becoming more involved in the past few years, KSE solidly backed their manager and recruitment team. Arsenal broke transfer records to bring in critical players to upgrade the team, like their action man midfielder Declan Rice. There have been occasions when the coach, Mikel Arteta, has wanted a specific deal and they have sanctioned it. In general they leave the football experts to make the technical and tactical assessments, then do their own financial checks before signing off on any deal. Where necessary Josh Kroenke will step in to assist in any negotiations.
Baugh: The Avalanche nailed a series of lottery draft picks to build their 2022 championship team and the contending teams around it. Nathan MacKinnon (No. 1 overall in 2013) and Cale Makar (No. 4 in 2017) were the crown jewels, but Colorado also hit on captain Gabriel Landeskog (No. 2 in 2011), Mikko Rantanen (No. 10 in 2015) and to some degree Bowen Byram (No. 4 in 2019).…

full_text:
Aaron Donald joins a Rams defense that added All-Pro talent in the secondary and along the D-line in the offseason. Kirby Lee / Imagn Images
LOS ANGELES — Aaron Donald walked onto the field at the Los Angeles Rams’ practice facility on Sunday and glanced at 52 other players he’ll now call teammates. He took a moment to let it sink in.
“Man, this is wild,” he told defensive back Quentin Lake.
This is finally starting to feel real to Donald and to the Rams’ defenders. The three-time Defensive Player of the Year is back after two years of retirement.
But as Donald, 35, spends the next couple of weeks ramping up to see if he can return to the first-team All-Pro level he was at in 2023, he also knows he’s not coming back to the same squad.
This one is no longer looking at him to fill the impact lost by Jalen Ramsey in a post-Super Bowl retool. If he can get back to being a star again, he’ll be one of a few on a defense that’s been supercharged in a single offseason.
It’s a mystery what this will look like when Donald is ready to rush the passer from the interior as Myles Garrett crashes down from the edge and Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson play in coverage while seven other returning starters from a top-10 defense try to fit around them.
This time, the unknown is exciting.
“The first thing that goes through your mind is, ‘Teams probably hate us,'” Lake said. “All of these other teams probably hate us. We’re like the new Dodgers.”
It’s hard to know exactly how dominant a defensive line with Garrett and Donald will be or how opposing offenses will react to it. The idea was so fascinating that the blockbuster trade for Garrett became the biggest factor in getting Donald to consider a return.
“We’re teammates now,” Donald said with a grin. “Hopefully we can do some special things together.”
It’s also never happened before. Garrett and Donald will represent the NFL’s first-ever pairing of two players with at least 100 career sacks and a 20-sack season under their belts, according to Sports Reference.
When Donald last played for the Rams, the game plan was straightforward.
“It brings clarity,” defensive lineman Kobie Turner said. “When I was playing with him (in 2023), and they slid the front to him, you knew what your job was and exactly how you have to execute it. When you have clarity, you’re able to use that clarity.
“Sean (McVay) talks about, ‘Our clarity, their confusion.’ You’re able to play off of that, you’re able to know exactly what your task is and you’re able to play together as a full unit as well to create confusion for the offense.”
But Garrett brought the same manipulation numbers to a Cleveland Browns defense that consistently finished in the top 10. That unit didn’t have as much help in the pass rush around him, which let Garrett play through those double-teams and sliding protections to still create 23 sacks in 2025, the most in a single season in NFL history.
Now, the Rams will have two of them on the defensive line. Garrett will often play the right end position, over the left tackle, with Donald flanking him to the inside at the 3-technique spot. The two are big enough and athletic enough to be able to switch alignments at times, or to do so after the snap with stunts that loop Garrett inside and Donald around the edge. They can even line Garrett up over the center like a middle linebacker on an A-gap blitz, as the Browns did at times under defensive coordinator Jim Schwartz.
“That’s going to be the question: Where are they going to send the slide to? How are they going to be able to help?” Turner said.
“If they want to play game and start switching up the slides and giving different people one-on-ones and giving Myles one-on-ones and oh, by the way, me and B.Y. (Byron Young) and (Braden) Fiske, that’s going to be trouble for them. They’re going to have to be able to figure out their plan at some point.”
Donald and Garrett will command such attention that it’ll be easy to forget that Turner and Young have both racked up at least seven sacks in three straight seasons. Last year, Young played opposite Jared Verse as Verse began to command those sliding protections and double-teams, and Young responded to one-on-one matchups and quarterbacks bailing to his side with a 12-sack season and his first Pro Bowl appearance.
He’s hungry for even more in a contract year.
“I need to get to All-Pro,” Young said. “I need to be a guy where when it comes to that third down-and-long, and we need to have it, I come through. I’ll force a bad play or force a bad decision. That’s what it is for me. I want to be that guy where they look to find, ‘OK, we need a stop. We’re behind. Or we need to seal the deal.’ I want to be one of those crunch-time situation guys.”
The Rams led the NFL last season in pressure rate out of four-man rushes, according to the NFL’s Next Gen Stats, and that came without either Garrett or Donald.
“You could almost rush just those two guys and drop everyone else back in coverage and see what happens,” Lake said. “That’d be pretty funny.”
Unlike last year, the Rams are not asking the front four to create so much havoc that they have to overcome a lack of investment at outside cornerback. That model ended up becoming Los Angeles’ Achilles’ heel in the second half of last season and into the playoffs, as offenses found quick passes, downfield perimeter throws and perimeter runs that exposed slender cornerbacks Emmanuel Forbes Jr. and Cobie Durant.
So when the Rams traded for a two-time All-Pro in McDuffie, as well as his Kansas City Chiefs running mate in Watson, they weren’t just adding two players with two Super Bowl titles. They were targeting specific archetypes of physical run stoppers and press-man coverage options.
Their presence will force teams to stop chasing perimeter runs to escape Garrett and Donald, as well as nose tackle Poona Ford and linebacker Nate Landman, who arrived last season to shore up the middle of the run defense.
Without easy quick throws against cornerbacks playing off coverage, more targets should come the way of Lake and strong safety Kam Curl, whom the Rams believed in enough to sign for $49 million combined in guarantees over the past year.
Those two can then move around more to disguise their intentions and locations. Whereas the Rams have one question mark on defense at the cover linebacker spot, Curl could offer a replacement for Omar Speights in that spot when the Rams play in dime, as they did more than any other defense last season.
Lake will be able to rotate from nickel cornerback to free safety to strong safety with the addition of McDuffie, who will slide inside at his best position at nickel at times in order to be closer to the ball. McDuffie has eight forced fumbles since he was drafted in 2022.
The biggest beneficiary could be the starting defensive back the Rams have yet to pay. Kam Kinchens enters his third year at age 23, and he’ll play in more of a downhill attacking mode, chasing tips and overthrows from quarterbacks sped up by Garrett, Donald, Turner and Young while avoiding the physical coverage of McDuffie and Watson.
A similar style allowed Kinchens to rack up 11 interceptions in his final two seasons at the University of Miami and four more as a rookie with the Rams in 2024, before he spent last season cleaning up more mistakes by outside cornerbacks.
“To have a roster this talented is almost unheard of,” Lake said. “It’s important for us as a team to understand it’s every given Sunday, regardless of whether you have the talent or not. I have the true belief that we’re going to be able to continue to work and be able to do it.”
Perhaps the greatest overall shift is the impact the additions of Garrett, Donald, McDuffie and Watson have had on the defense’s floor and optionality.
Now, rather than covering No. 1 wide receivers, Forbes can slide into a third outside cornerback role as an option in dime sets when McDuffie slides inside. Pass rushers such as Fiske and Josaiah Stewart,…

title: NFL execs rank NFC teams: Rams, Seahawks clear favorites. Can the Bears keep rising? Mike Sando 60
summary:
Matthew Stafford's Rams spent the offseason loading up after falling to the Seahawks in the NFC Championship Game. (Simon Bruty / Sports Illustrated via Getty Images)
With the NFL preseason finished, it’s time to check in with team executives to set expectations for the coming 2026 season one final time.
The six executives polled this week ranked teams 1-16 in each conference, under the condition of anonymity to allow them to speak freely. I also asked them to place each team into four buckets:
full_text:
Matthew Stafford's Rams spent the offseason loading up after falling to the Seahawks in the NFC Championship Game. (Simon Bruty / Sports Illustrated via Getty Images)
With the NFL preseason finished, it’s time to check in with team executives to set expectations for the coming 2026 season one final time.
The six executives polled this week ranked teams 1-16 in each conference, under the condition of anonymity to allow them to speak freely. I also asked them to place each team into four buckets: Super Bowl contenders, division contenders, sub-.500 teams and likely top-10 pickers in the 2027 draft.
We start with the NFC, where the Seattle Seahawks are reigning champs, but the Los Angeles Rams are the strong betting favorite. One of the execs had the Chicago Bears atop his ballot, on the thinking that seasons rarely play out as expected. Teams are ranked below in median order, with average as a tiebreaker.
Votes: 2-1-1-1-1-2 | Avg: 1.3 | Median: 1 | Vegas wins: 11.5 (1st-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 6
All but two voters moved the Rams to the top of the NFC after an offseason that saw Los Angeles overhaul its defense with Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald and two cornerbacks from Kansas City.
"I think they are the best team in the NFC by far," a former GM said. "Beyond all the defensive additions, Matthew Stafford is just surgical. So impressive."
The Rams went 1-2 against Seattle last season largely because they finished those games with a -26.7 EPA differential on special teams.
"It is hard for me to go against Seattle being the top team in the NFC," the voter putting the Seahawks atop the conference said. "Talent-wise, it is going to be really close."
One other voter had the Bears first, partly on the theory that things tend to play out unexpectedly.
"I would say there is a clear gap (between the Rams and the rest of the NFC) with the return of Aaron Donald," another voter said.
The Rams are the strongest preseason Super Bowl favorite since 2002, per covers.com.
"I think Myles Garrett puts them over the top," another exec said.
Votes: 1-2-3-2-2-6 | Avg: 2.7 | Median: 2 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 5 | Division contender: 1
The Seahawks have an unproven offensive coordinator (Brian Fleury) after Klint Kubiak's departure to become the Raiders' coach. They spent their offseason extending key players (Leonard Williams, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Devon Witherspoon) while the Rams were adding big names from the outside. The cornerback situation remains a worry, and it's unclear whether their top defensive chess piece, Nick Emmanwori, will be at his best physically following ankle surgery.
"It's hard for me to see them continuing to get better now that they are a marked man," one exec said. "A lot of people got paid. Is the hunger still there?"
The transition from hunter to hunted affects every Super Bowl winner.
"I don't know about Super Bowl, but they are going to go deep in the playoffs," another exec said. "I think them and the Packers are probably the next (NFC) teams after L.A."
Voters trust Seattle's defense while taking a wait-and-see approach with the offense.
"It is hard for me to think you're not going to have some kind of dropoff going from Kubiak to Fleury, even if it is in the same schematic realm," one voter said. "You lost Kubiak, you lost the Super Bowl MVP (Kenneth Walker III). I know you're excited about Jadarian Price, but …"
Votes: 3-4-5-3-3-4 | Avg: 3.7 | Median: 3.5 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 4 | Division contender: 2
With Seattle on "Hard Knocks" and the Rams making splash after splash this offseason, the Eagles are about as under the radar as can be. Reminder: Philly leads the league in regular-season victories over the past four seasons (50) while ranking second to Kansas City in postseason wins (six).
"They could go either way, to be quite honest," one exec said of the Eagles, who finished 11-6 last season. "I think they will be better. The thing that was really good for them is a potential concern, and that is the receiver position and running back. Saquon (Barkley) did not have a great year. The offensive line health and age is a concern. They will still be formidable."
Will A.J. Brown's departure be addition by subtraction? One voter said the pressure's on quarterback Jalen Hurts, whose relationship with Brown had grown cold and who will be playing in an overhauled offensive system under new coordinator Sean Mannion.
"It was hard for me to ding Philly even if the offense is unknown, even if they are taking a step back without A.J. Brown," another exec said. "Vic Fangio and that defense is going to be top five. That O-line is going to be pretty good. It is still Saquon Barkley. Could they win 16-13 every week? Probably."
Votes: 5-8-2-4-4-3 | Avg: 4.3 | Median: 4 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-6th-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 3 | Division contender: 3
All agree the Cowboys' offense appears formidable. How much can the defense improve?
"Anything is better than what they did last year on defense," the voter placing Dallas second in the NFC said. "They shocked the system by trading Micah Parsons, and I just think generally speaking, new coordinators on defense create variance."
No team is seeking greater variance on defense from last season than the Cowboys, who ranked 32 nd in EPA per play by a wide margin, per TruMedia. They replaced Matt Eberflus with first-time coordinator Christian Parker.
"Quinnen Williams is good, and they have a little more girth up front, so it should be better, but they've got some unknowns there too with coaches and philosophy," the voter ranking Dallas eighth said.
The voter ranking Dallas fifth thought the Cowboys' defense might outrank the Packers' defense, notable in light of the Parsons trade last year.
"I like the coordinator," this voter said of Parker. "He is going to help maximize what they have. The secondary is still not a strength, but they have an impressive front seven."
Linebacker DeMarvion Overshown's health is a key variable multiple voters highlighted.
"I have defensive concerns, for sure," one said. "Do they have enough pass rush? How healthy is Overshown? How good are the corners? But they did address the interior with Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark, and I like Caleb Downs. They will be better up the middle."
Votes: 4-7-6-7-5-1 | Avg: 5.0 | Median: 5.5 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-6th-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 2 | Division contender: 4
The one voter ranking Chicago atop the NFC said the Bears have an elite coach in Ben Johnson, a rising, super-talented quarterback in Caleb Williams and enough talent to take another step.
"I know all the regression stuff," this voter said, alluding to the Bears' ability to win seven games last season after trailing in the final two minutes. "The coach is really good, they have a really good ascending quarterback, the roster is super talented. They did all the right things in the offseason to fight the regression."
The top three teams in the NFC North are tightly bunched in these rankings.
"I love the whole NFC North," one voter said, "but the top three all have defensive concerns."
New safety Coby Bryant's season-ending knee injury hurts Chicago. The Bears still have uncertainty at left tackle.
"Can they win a playoff game again?" an exec asked. "Sure, but I guess that's where I cap the Super Bowl contender of like, do I see them coming out of the NFC over the Rams? I can't see it. Kyle (Shanahan), (Brock) Purdy and the Niners, they have been there, done that. Even Detroit, I trust."
Another voter thought the Bears' rise under Johnson last season painted a target on their backs heading into 2026.

full_text:
Sam Darnold and the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks open the season behind the Los Angeles Rams on oddsboards. Sean M. Haffey / Getty Images
The top of the NFC West oddsboard looks a lot like the top of the Super Bowl oddsboard: The Los Angeles Rams are favored and the reigning champion Seattle Seahawks follow.
The strength of the Rams is the simple answer as to why the Seahawks aren’t favored to defend either of those titles — but we’ve asked The Athletic’s predictive analyst, Austin Mock, to break down how his model projects both teams.
The Rams are certainly overpriced in the betting market, but they’re rightfully favored to dethrone the Seahawks in the NFC West.
In a normal year, the Seahawks would likely be favored to defend their titles. Unfortunately for them, the Rams put together an offseason for the ages to improve a roster that already gave the reigning champs all they could handle in 2025.
Last year, my model actually gave the edge to the Rams as the best team in the NFL, but the Seahawks cliched home-field advantage throughout the NFC playoffs to give them the inside track to another ring. A lot has changed since then, though, with the Seahawks losing a few players — most notably Kenneth Walker III, Boye Mafe and Riq Woolen — while the Rams added superstar pass rusher Myles Garrett and All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie. Oh, and Aaron Donald just came out of retirement to join Garrett on what could be one of the best defensive lines in NFL history.
I personally believe Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald to be one of the brightest defensive minds in football — he’s pretty high in my ranking of head coaches — but we’ll have to wait and see if new offensive coordinator Brian Fleury can pick up where Klint Kubiak left off before taking the head-coaching job in Las Vegas. Fleury has no play-calling experience, which breeds even more uncertainty around the continuity from last season.
Going back-to-back is tough, but it’s even harder when you already play in the best division in football and a super team formed as your biggest competitor. So my model isn’t necessarily knocking the Seahawks — in fact, it has them as the second-best team in football — the gap between them and the Rams just grew bigger this offseason. For perspective, the distance between two is the same as the distance between the Seahawks at No. 2 and the Philadelphia Eagles at No. 7.

There is change at the top, too. Nolan Teasley is the new general manager, hired in June following 13 seasons in Seattle. But the Vikings have continuity on the sideline. Kevin O’Connell is in his fifth season as head coach, with Brian Flores returning for a fourth running the defense.
Meanwhile, the offensive core remains largely intact. Aaron Jones Sr. and Jordan Mason line up in the backfield. Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison and T.J. Hockenson are reliable targets, along with free-agent addition Jauan Jennings. Still, the pressure point is quarterback: Minnesota needs Murray to settle in quickly. The No. 1 pick in the 2019 NFL Draft is trying to rebound with a new team, one that is seeking its first postseason victory in seven years.
Vikings games are scattered across CBS, Fox, ESPN, NBC and Prime Video this year, with late-season broadcast windows still in flux. Minnesota also heads to Estadio Banorte in Week 11 to face the San Francisco 49ers, the franchise’s first game in Mexico. full_text:
When Mike Vrabel says he doesn't think the Patriots are a "deep team," he's also trying to leave last season behind. Edward Finan / Imagn Images via Reuters Connect
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — To selectively monitor Mike Vrabel’s media availabilities this summer is to come away believing the 2026 New England Patriots will be lucky to win four games. Who could forget this instant classic, delivered last Saturday night after New England’s preseason game against the Philadelphia Eagles: “I do not think we have a very deep team.”
At first glance, or listen, it must have been a little gasp-inducing for Patriots fans. What!? The defending AFC champions lack depth?
But then came the all-important second glance, after which, it’s safe to say, most Pats fans understood where Vrabel was coming from. As The Athletic ’s Chad Graff pointed out, Vrabel wasn’t criticizing the front office but pointing out several years of questionable drafting by various regimes. It also explains why Vrabel was extra, extra cautious about how and when he used his starters during the preseason, all the better to protect his assets going into the season opener next week in Seattle.
But if we can put aside the specifics of Vrabel’s preseason quotage and instead do a big-picture analysis, a pattern emerges: What Vrabel has been saying, over and over and over, is that the 2026 Patriots have won nothing . The team that shocked the oddsmakers in 2025 by going 14-3 … that team no longer exists. The team that advanced all the way to Super Bowl LX before being chloroformed by the Seahawks … that team no longer exists. The hallway hugs delivered by Vrabel to his victorious players? If you want another hug, win a game first.
True, most coaches and managers take this attitude during the run-up to a new season following a season that was hugely successful and entertaining. And yet I’m always surprised when teams are quite comfortable showing off last year’s championship bling when they show up for a new season. Remember what happened after the 2018 Red Sox chewed up the postseason competition en route to winning Boston’s fourth World Series championship this century? Four months later, when the Sox arrived in Fort Myers, Fla., to limber up for a new season, it was as though they were still popping champagne corks on the Dodger Stadium infield.
And Alex Cora, who was managing the Red Sox at the time, had no problem with that.
“You turn the page because something negative happened,” Cora said during spring training in 2019. “And there’s nothing negative from 2018.”
What was negative was that the 2019 Red Sox went 84-78 and failed to make the postseason. While it’d be a reach to blame the failure solely on anything said during spring training, it’s not unfair to say that the 2019 Red Sox were not a collection of hungry, eye-of-the-tiger types. And I write these words as someone who believes Cora is a fine manager who will be back in the game before the calendar year is out.
Bill Belichick is the patron saint of leaving past seasons where they belong, which is in the past. Every summer, from the moment he’d empty the bag of footballs on the first day of training camp, it was no longer permissible to talk about past championships.
Belichick famously broke his own rule when, in March 2023, he reached for his resume after being asked by a reporter if he could say something that would give Patriots fans a reason to be optimistic for the upcoming season. “The last 25 years,” Belichick said, as if all those seasons of deep playoff runs and Super Bowl victories were all Pats fans needed to get excited for the 2023 season.
Belichick was, and is, one of the greatest coaches in NFL history. But the 2023 Pats went 4-13, and they went 4-13 because they were a lousy team. The previous 25 years didn’t help one bit. Belichick was fired, after which came one-and-done Jerod Mayo and another 4-13 campaign. And then came Vrabel, and a shocker of a 2025 season in which the Pats went 14-3 and advanced to the Super Bowl.
That catches us up. It’s 2026, and the Patriots have won nothing. What’s more, says Vrabel, “I do not think we have a very deep team.”
Belichick also had a way of using a simple declarative sentence to avoid talking about uncomfortable recent events. And then he’d keep using that simple declarative sentence until everybody in the room was lulled to sleep. In 2014, for example, a couple of days after the Pats were handed a 41-14 beating by the Kansas City Chiefs, Belichick signaled he was moving on from that mess by answering every question with, “We’re on to Cincinnati.”
In 2016, it was, “We’re on to Seattle” after Belichick was asked repeatedly if he had written a letter that then-presidential candidate Donald Trump read aloud at a rally in Manchester, N.H.
Vrabel, meeting with the media Tuesday afternoon at the team’s training facility in Foxborough, pulled a similar rabbit out of his hat:
Reporter: “Mike, I know you guys are still constructing and tinkering with the roster, but do you feel that the core of it right now, the 53, could compete for another Super Bowl?”
Cagey answer: “We’re focused on just competing against Seattle, not competing for something that’s going to happen in February. We’re really just trying to indoctrinate and onboard these new players to understand our language, our terminology, how we practice.”
The Patriots’ 2025 season does not exist. Nor does the next Super Bowl.
The Patriots are on to Seattle.

full_text:
Levon Kirkland played in the NFL from 1992 to 2002, mostly with the Pittsburgh Steelers. Photo by George Gojkovich / Getty Images
This story is part of Peak, The Athletic’s desk covering the mental side of sports. Sign up for Peak’s newsletter here .
Levon Kirkland played 11 seasons in the NFL from 1992 to 2002, mostly with the Pittsburgh Steelers. He now works in the Clemson athletic department.
These are the three best leaders he played with:
He knew how to set the atmosphere for our defense. He was the guy we all followed because he set such a high standard physically for all of us.
We had some great guys on that defense: Rod Woodson, Carnell Lake, Darren Perry. But I thought Greg really set the temperature for all of us, and we played at his tone.
He was a third-degree black belt who came out of Fort Valley State, a small HBCU. He was one of the hardest workers I’ve ever seen on the football field. He showed us what determination and hard work were all about.
When practice was over, we were pretty much done. There was nothing the coaches really wanted us to do. But Greg would lead us to this hill at training camp, and we would run hills.
We had two practices a day back then: one in the morning and one in the afternoon. That second practice was usually full pads, with a lot of thudding and hitting.
That’s when he would take us to the hill — and it was a steep hill. We all did it without complaining, and it was Greg who urged us to do that.
No supervision, no one telling us to do it but Greg. And we ran as many as he thought we should run.
The year we went to the Super Bowl in 1996, he really made it a point that we all got together. Offense, defense, Black, White. We all went to this bar across the street from the stadium and hung out.
I really felt the reason we went to the Super Bowl was that we had a better connection with each other.
He was such a great leader because he led by example.
He was really mild-mannered, but he was one of the best players I’ve ever seen in my life. I looked up to him: the way he worked, the way he carried himself.
I really feel like his identity was why he performed so well. He knew who he was, and he wasn’t going to change for anybody.
He just had purpose in what he did; he did it day in and day out, and I feel like that purpose gave him an advantage.
He led with his play and actions. I remember we played in the AFC Championship Game. At the time, it was almost unheard of to have a center who could snap the ball and still pull to one side or the other. I remember he snapped the ball to Kordell Stewart, pulled and clocked someone, and we scored on the play.
That was leadership because he set the tone.
One of his leadership qualities was his unselfishness.
He was one of the most established safeties in the NFL at the time, but he ended up playing cornerback for us the same year we went to the Super Bowl.
Now, that’s a tough transition to move from safety to cornerback. Most guys would have said, “No, bring in another corner. I’m going to play my spot where I’m comfortable.”
So it really showed how much he cared about the team. It showed me that sometimes you have to get out of your comfort zone and sometimes you have to do what’s best for the team.
That’s what he did without any complaints, without any grumbling, without any noise.
To me, that was tremendous leadership.

full_text:
It was only three games, but Jason Myers' struggles this August could foreshadow more problems, as he experienced in 2017. Jay Biggerstaff / Imagn Images
Just seven months ago, Jason Myers put the finishing touches on one of the finest seasons by a kicker in NFL history.
After hitting all five field goal attempts for the Seattle Seahawks in their Super Bowl LX win in February, Myers became the first player in NFL history to score 200 points in a season (including playoffs).
But during three Seahawks preseason games this August, Myers made only 4 of 9 kicks: 2 of 5 field goal attempts — including a would-be game-winner from 52 yards in the finale — and 2 of 4 extra point attempts. That total of 11 points lost on kicks tied for the fourth-most in a preseason since 2000, per TruMedia. Measuring by expected points added, which factors in the difficulty of kicks, Myers cost Seattle 7.4 EPA, eighth-worst in that span.
The 35-year-old’s recent struggles have yet to reach the point of panic for Seattle. Should they carry over into the regular season, though, that could quickly change.
Myers has been nails since joining the Seahawks in 2019, converting over 86.2 percent of his field goal attempts (200 for 232) in 117 regular-season games and making the Pro Bowl in 2022.
Still, his shaky preseason — and the way Myers missed the kicks: four wide right and one shanked to the left — has brought unwanted attention to Seattle’s special teams, which last season were among the best in the league.
It’s just preseason. No time to overreact, right? Well, there are many reasons to believe Myers’ rough patch is an anomaly … but there is also evidence to suggest it is cause for concern.
Myers himself is quite familiar with how a rotten preseason can foreshadow a trying regular season.
In 2017 with the Jacksonville Jaguars, his third year in the NFL, Myers went 4 of 7 on field goal attempts and 7 of 8 extra point attempts in four exhibition games. After he missed two field goals in a 10-point loss to the Los Angeles Rams in October, he was cut, finishing 11 of 15 on field goals and 15 of 17 on PATs in six games that season. Myers worked out for other teams but did not join another roster until 2018.
He quickly rebounded, landing with the New York Jets and making 33 of 36 field goal attempts to earn Pro Bowl honors. His 91.7 percent conversion rate that season remains the third-highest of his career. That led to a four-year, $15.5 million contract with Seattle in 2019.
Myers is now in his 12th NFL season and eighth with Seattle. Aside from this August, he has been excellent in exhibition games since joining the Seahawks, going 29 of 33 (87.9 percent) over the previous six preseasons.
Other kickers have turned dismal preseasons into aberrations, too. But that’s not the norm.
In 2018, a 28-year-old Justin Tucker made only 4 of 8 field goal attempts in the preseason for the Baltimore Ravens, though all four misses were from 51 yards or longer (including one that was blocked). In the regular season, he made 35 of 39 kicks (90 percent) en route to being named a first-team All-Pro for the third time in his career.
A year later, then-35-year-old Stephen Gostkowski missed three field goals from 43 yards or shorter in the preseason for the New England Patriots. The five-time NFL scoring leader was sharper in the regular season, converting 7 of 8 field goal attempts, but he missed four PATs before needing season-ending hip surgery. The Patriots released him after the season, and he played only one more in the NFL.
A few other kickers, like Matt Prater with the Detroit Lions in 2018, have weathered a rough preseason. But there aren't many who have hit similar depths and pulled through.
From 2000 to 2025, 18 kickers posted an EPA of minus-4.9 or worse on field goals and extra points in one preseason, per TruMedia. Fourteen were cut or released within two months. Some latched on with other teams, but seven of the 14 never appeared in another regular-season game. Only six produced positive EPA in the regular season. Most of the 18 were younger players, but some were experienced veterans and many were once highly touted.
Typical disclaimers about preseason cite weaker competition, watered-down schemes and small sample sizes, but the first two factors don’t apply to kickers. Nine kicks is certainly a small sample size, but the 26 years of data above isn’t encouraging.
Perhaps it helps Myers that he has been here before, albeit nine years ago. His job security has rarely been called into question during his tenure in the Emerald City, and rightfully so.
Last season, he passed Norm Johnson as Seattle's all-time leading scorer with 892 points. He has signed two four-year contracts with the Seahawks, including an extension worth $5.3 million annually (second-highest in the NFL at the time) shortly after his Pro Bowl 2022 season.
And yet, Myers is entering a contract year. He'll be called upon quite frequently once the Seahawks start their title defense with their season opener on Sept. 9, a Super Bowl rematch against the New England Patriots.
In two of the past three seasons, Myers has led the NFL in field goal attempts, with 42 in 2023 and 48 in 2025. Depending on how quarterback Sam Darnold, wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba and the rest of the Seahawks offense adjust to first-year offensive coordinator Brian Fleury, opportunities could run aplenty for Myers.
Can he figure out what's ailing him and quickly remedy the issue? He was critical to the second championship in franchise history and will need to be at his best if the Seahawks want to become the 10th team to repeat as the Super Bowl winner.
Otherwise, Myers could find himself in a spot quite similar to where he was nearly a decade ago in Jacksonville.

summary:

With the NFL preseason finished, it’s time to check in with team executives to set expectations for the coming 2026 season one final time.

full_text:
Matthew Stafford's Rams spent the offseason loading up after falling to the Seahawks in the NFC Championship Game. (Simon Bruty / Sports Illustrated via Getty Images)
With the NFL preseason finished, it’s time to check in with team executives to set expectations for the coming 2026 season one final time.
The six executives polled this week ranked teams 1-16 in each conference, under the condition of anonymity to allow them to speak freely. I also asked them to place each team into four buckets: Super Bowl contenders, division contenders, sub-.500 teams and likely top-10 pickers in the 2027 draft.
We start with the NFC, where the Seattle Seahawks are reigning champs, but the Los Angeles Rams are the strong betting favorite. One of the execs had the Chicago Bears atop his ballot, on the thinking that seasons rarely play out as expected. Teams are ranked below in median order, with average as a tiebreaker.
Votes: 2-1-1-1-1-2 | Avg: 1.3 | Median: 1 | Vegas wins: 11.5 (1st-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 6
All but two voters moved the Rams to the top of the NFC after an offseason that saw Los Angeles overhaul its defense with Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald and two cornerbacks from Kansas City.
"I think they are the best team in the NFC by far," a former GM said. "Beyond all the defensive additions, Matthew Stafford is just surgical. So impressive."
The Rams went 1-2 against Seattle last season largely because they finished those games with a -26.7 EPA differential on special teams.
"It is hard for me to go against Seattle being the top team in the NFC," the voter putting the Seahawks atop the conference said. "Talent-wise, it is going to be really close."
One other voter had the Bears first, partly on the theory that things tend to play out unexpectedly.
"I would say there is a clear gap (between the Rams and the rest of the NFC) with the return of Aaron Donald," another voter said.
The Rams are the strongest preseason Super Bowl favorite since 2002, per covers.com.
"I think Myles Garrett puts them over the top," another exec said.
Votes: 1-2-3-2-2-6 | Avg: 2.7 | Median: 2 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 5 | Division contender: 1
The Seahawks have an unproven offensive coordinator (Brian Fleury) after Klint Kubiak's departure to become the Raiders' coach. They spent their offseason extending key players (Leonard Williams, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Devon Witherspoon) while the Rams were adding big names from the outside. The cornerback situation remains a worry, and it's unclear whether their top defensive chess piece, Nick Emmanwori, will be at his best physically following ankle surgery.
"It's hard for me to see them continuing to get better now that they are a marked man," one exec said. "A lot of people got paid. Is the hunger still there?"
The transition from hunter to hunted affects every Super Bowl winner.
"I don't know about Super Bowl, but they are going to go deep in the playoffs," another exec said. "I think them and the Packers are probably the next (NFC) teams after L.A."
Voters trust Seattle's defense while taking a wait-and-see approach with the offense.
"It is hard for me to think you're not going to have some kind of dropoff going from Kubiak to Fleury, even if it is in the same schematic realm," one voter said. "You lost Kubiak, you lost the Super Bowl MVP (Kenneth Walker III). I know you're excited about Jadarian Price, but …"
Votes: 3-4-5-3-3-4 | Avg: 3.7 | Median: 3.5 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 4 | Division contender: 2
With Seattle on "Hard Knocks" and the Rams making splash after splash this offseason, the Eagles are about as under the radar as can be. Reminder: Philly leads the league in regular-season victories over the past four seasons (50) while ranking second to Kansas City in postseason wins (six).
"They could go either way, to be quite honest," one exec said of the Eagles, who finished 11-6 last season. "I think they will be better. The thing that was really good for them is a potential concern, and that is the receiver position and running back. Saquon (Barkley) did not have a great year. The offensive line health and age is a concern. They will still be formidable."
Will A.J. Brown's departure be addition by subtraction? One voter said the pressure's on quarterback Jalen Hurts, whose relationship with Brown had grown cold and who will be playing in an overhauled offensive system under new coordinator Sean Mannion.
"It was hard for me to ding Philly even if the offense is unknown, even if they are taking a step back without A.J. Brown," another exec said. "Vic Fangio and that defense is going to be top five. That O-line is going to be pretty good. It is still Saquon Barkley. Could they win 16-13 every week? Probably."
Votes: 5-8-2-4-4-3 | Avg: 4.3 | Median: 4 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-6th-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 3 | Division contender: 3
All agree the Cowboys' offense appears formidable. How much can the defense improve?
"Anything is better than what they did last year on defense," the voter placing Dallas second in the NFC said. "They shocked the system by trading Micah Parsons, and I just think generally speaking, new coordinators on defense create variance."
No team is seeking greater variance on defense from last season than the Cowboys, who ranked 32 nd in EPA per play by a wide margin, per TruMedia. They replaced Matt Eberflus with first-time coordinator Christian Parker.
"Quinnen Williams is good, and they have a little more girth up front, so it should be better, but they've got some unknowns there too with coaches and philosophy," the voter ranking Dallas eighth said.
The voter ranking Dallas fifth thought the Cowboys' defense might outrank the Packers' defense, notable in light of the Parsons trade last year.
"I like the coordinator," this voter said of Parker. "He is going to help maximize what they have. The secondary is still not a strength, but they have an impressive front seven."
Linebacker DeMarvion Overshown's health is a key variable multiple voters highlighted.
"I have defensive concerns, for sure," one said. "Do they have enough pass rush? How healthy is Overshown? How good are the corners? But they did address the interior with Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark, and I like Caleb Downs. They will be better up the middle."
Votes: 4-7-6-7-5-1 | Avg: 5.0 | Median: 5.5 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-6th-NFC)
Tier votes: SB contender: 2 | Division contender: 4
The one voter ranking Chicago atop the NFC said the Bears have an elite coach in Ben Johnson, a rising, super-talented quarterback in Caleb Williams and enough talent to take another step.
"I know all the regression stuff," this voter said, alluding to the Bears' ability to win seven games last season after trailing in the final two minutes. "The coach is really good, they have a really good ascending quarterback, the roster is super talented. They did all the right things in the offseason to fight the regression."
The top three teams in the NFC North are tightly bunched in these rankings.
"I love the whole NFC North," one voter said, "but the top three all have defensive concerns."
New safety Coby Bryant's season-ending knee injury hurts Chicago. The Bears still have uncertainty at left tackle.
"Can they win a playoff game again?" an exec asked. "Sure, but I guess that's where I cap the Super Bowl contender of like, do I see them coming out of the NFC over the Rams? I can't see it. Kyle (Shanahan), (Brock) Purdy and the Niners, they have been there, done that. Even Detroit, I trust."
Another voter thought the Bears' rise under Johnson last season painted a target on their backs heading into 2026.
"I'm going to double down on them," the exec placing the Bears fourth in the NFC said. "They are not going to catch people by surprise this year, and the NFC North will be tough. I still think they'll be OK."

full_text:
Sam Darnold and the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks open the season behind the Los Angeles Rams on oddsboards. Sean M. Haffey / Getty Images
The top of the NFC West oddsboard looks a lot like the top of the Super Bowl oddsboard: The Los Angeles Rams are favored and the reigning champion Seattle Seahawks follow.
The strength of the Rams is the simple answer as to why the Seahawks aren’t favored to defend either of those titles — but we’ve asked The Athletic’s predictive analyst, Austin Mock, to break down how his model projects both teams.
The Rams are certainly overpriced in the betting market, but they’re rightfully favored to dethrone the Seahawks in the NFC West.
In a normal year, the Seahawks would likely be favored to defend their titles. Unfortunately for them, the Rams put together an offseason for the ages to improve a roster that already gave the reigning champs all they could handle in 2025.
Last year, my model actually gave the edge to the Rams as the best team in the NFL, but the Seahawks cliched home-field advantage throughout the NFC playoffs to give them the inside track to another ring. A lot has changed since then, though, with the Seahawks losing a few players — most notably Kenneth Walker III, Boye Mafe and Riq Woolen — while the Rams added superstar pass rusher Myles Garrett and All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie. Oh, and Aaron Donald just came out of retirement to join Garrett on what could be one of the best defensive lines in NFL history.
I personally believe Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald to be one of the brightest defensive minds in football — he’s pretty high in my ranking of head coaches — but we’ll have to wait and see if new offensive coordinator Brian Fleury can pick up where Klint Kubiak left off before taking the head-coaching job in Las Vegas. Fleury has no play-calling experience, which breeds even more uncertainty around the continuity from last season.
Going back-to-back is tough, but it’s even harder when you already play in the best division in football and a super team formed as your biggest competitor. So my model isn’t necessarily knocking the Seahawks — in fact, it has them as the second-best team in football — the gap between them and the Rams just grew bigger this offseason. For perspective, the distance between two is the same as the distance between the Seahawks at No. 2 and the Philadelphia Eagles at No. 7.

full_text:
The 49ers' fans travel well everywhere, even to a continent nearly 8,000 miles away. Thearon W. Henderson / Getty Images
The Los Angeles Rams might have avoided the annual migration of San Francisco 49ers fans to SoFi Stadium this year, but they’ll still be seeing red — a lot of it — at next week’s season opener in Australia, the NFL’s first game on the continent .
That’s because not only are 49ers fans the most well-traveled in the league, but there are already plenty of them Down Under. According to the NFL, the 49ers are the league’s most popular team in Australia, even though they aren’t one of the four teams — the Rams, Philadelphia Eagles, Las Vegas Raiders and Seattle Seahawks — with marketing rights in the country.
The 49ers leave for Melbourne on Wednesday night and arrive Friday morning. The Rams aren’t expected in until the day before the game, which kicks off locally at 10:35 a.m. on Sept. 11 (or 8:35 p.m. ET on Sept. 10).
“I think that comes from being one of the top teams in the ’80s, when a lot of people here consumed the NFL,” NFL Australia and New Zealand general manager Charlotte Offord said of the 49ers’ popularity. “And a lot of people continued to follow those top teams.”
Steve Moss, 50, will be among those wearing a 49ers jersey at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, which can host up to 100,024, next week. The Brisbane resident said his NFL introduction came in the early 1990s via the “John Madden American Football” video game he played on Sega Mega Drive, the Aussie equivalent of the Sega Genesis. The 49ers were winning Super Bowls, Joe Montana was a global figure and San Francisco became Moss’ team.
He said he drifted away from the sport over the next two decades as the 49ers slipped from their throne. But he came rushing back in 2015 when Jarryd Hayne, a star in the National Rugby League, won a roster spot with the 49ers.
“He was such an amazing Rugby League player,” Moss said. “It was a really huge story for him to make the roster. And so that’s when I really re-engaged with it.”
This time, Moss was hooked for good.
“As an adult, I could see the choreography and the work that goes into plays,” he said. “And it’s such a different style of football from the Australian code. But I found it fascinating. I paraphrase it like this: ‘I came back for Jarryd Hayne, and I stayed for Joe Staley.’”
For Australian fans like him, the NFL is a tangle of familiarity and foreignness.
The country already has its own brand of football, Australian rules football, a four-quarter game with hard hits, an oblong ball and uprights. The Australian Football League is the country’s most popular spectator sport, and half its 18 teams are based in Melbourne, one reason the city was tapped to host the 49ers and Rams. The AFL, in fact, will be in the midst of its postseason when the NFL comes to town.
Then again, concepts like a forward pass, polycarbonate helmets and the stop-and-start style of play are strange to Australian viewers. So is the sight of a player celebrating after nearly every play.
“A defensive guy gets a sack, and to us, he’s jumping around like he’s won the Super Bowl,” Moss said. “Every touchdown is a massive celebration. Even when teams are losing and they’ll score, they’ll celebrate. And that’s not what’s done over here. If you’re scoring, if you’re making good tackles, you’re just doing your job.”
Punter Jack Bouwmeester said Aussies call that “tall poppy syndrome.” Bouwmeester, a Bendigo, Australia, native who spent the offseason with the 49ers and is currently on the Rams’ practice squad, explained that in Australia, the poppy that strains for sunlight and rises above its mates is the one that gets lopped off.
“If anyone does anything good, they’ll cut you down for it,” he said. “Australia’s real humble. You’ve got to be humble — thank the team and everything.”
Said Moss: “The Australian reaction for someone who’s showboating too much is, ‘Oh, pull your head in, mate.’ I think it epitomizes the tall poppy syndrome — you’re sticking your head out too far.”
Still, Bouwmeester said that’s why some Australians are drawn to the NFL — because the Joe Staley – and George Kittle-sized personalities are so uncommon in their sports culture.
“In America you can kind of be yourself or puff your chest out a little bit,” said Bouwmeester, who played collegiately at Michigan State, Utah and Texas. “They like how people get in the postgame press conference and are like, ‘Oh, I dominated today.’ If you said that in Australia, it wouldn’t go down well.”
And plenty of Australians have been tuning in to the NFL over the past five years, which is why the league decided to hold a Week 1 game there. In 2022, the league had 5.7 million followers in Australia, Offord said. Last year, that number was 8.8 million — out of a population of roughly 28 million.
The league is actively marketing the sport in Australia (the Rams since 2021); flag football clinics and leagues have become popular; and fantasy football has caught on in a big way.
“People in this market love gambling on sports,” Offord said. “So I think there’s a correlation between those two.”
Said Bouwmeester: “All my closest friends do fantasy football. There’s also a lot more podcasts, a lot more people talking about it now than when I started punting (in 2018). Once they learn the game — and it was the same with Mom and Dad — it becomes a lot more enjoyable.”
Another reason the NFL has been able to catch on is that there isn’t much overlap between its season and the local rugby and football seasons. The AFL finishes in late September, and the NRL wraps up in October, around Week 5 of the NFL season. At that point, the NFL sees an uptick in Aussie interest that rises over the next three months, culminating with the Super Bowl. That game airs at 9:30 a.m. on a Monday.
“A few years ago, really diehard fans might watch it on their phone at work,” Moss said. “Now, people take the day off, there are watch parties, hotels get special licenses to be able to serve alcohol earlier in the morning. So, it’s definitely become a bigger thing over the last five years.”
Moss has been one of those diehards for the past decade or so, though he admits he’s usually at work when the 49ers are playing, and that when he watches the replays, he’ll fast-forward through stoppages and advertisements.
Next week’s game will be his first to watch in person. He’s looking forward to the strategy, the drama, the intensity and all the things that intrigue him about the NFL. But he’s not sure how his wife will react.
“I think she will love the atmosphere,” he said. “She won’t have a clue what’s going on as far as the intricacies of the match. But it’s gonna be such a great event. It seems like they’re putting in a lot of work for it, and Melbourne does events really well.”

title: What the Cardinals Final Roster Says About the Front Office's Vision
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals' final 53-man roster is settled, as prominent figures in head coach Mike LaFleur and general manager Monti Ossenfort pushed through a tough weekend of mass cuts and player evaluations to settle on what they believe are the best players to earn wins in 2026.
Whether that comes to fruition largely remains to be seen, though Arizona's initial group of 53 players is telling of the Cardinals, their front office, and what they envision for the future.
The Cardinals clearly weren't afraid to part with some vested players, either old or new to the team. Ranging from Sean Murphy-Bunting to Oli Udoh and more, there were several veterans the organization opted to bypass in exchange for youth and/or athleticism on the team.
Oftentimes, teams will simply roll with players that possess experience. That's even more prevalent for first-year head coaches — so for the Cardinals to cut 12 players with four years (or more) of experience with a new head coach, that's a vote of confidence in the younger crop of players.
Every healthy Cardinals rookie cracked the team's final roster — and the other two Cardinals on injured reserve in Kaleb Proctor and Chase Bisontis would have made it, too.
The Cardinals' influx of youth is a testament to Arizona's commitment to building through the draft under Ossenfort. 31 of the 53 players were drafted to the league since Ossenfort took over.
It's also a vote of confidence in Arizona's scouting department and LaFleur's staff to coach-up younger guys.
The Cardinals' special teams was sorely lacking last season, which led to the ultimate departure of coordinator Jeff Rodgers. In came Michael Ghobrial, who is looking to get Arizona's third phase back on track.
It's not uncommon for bottom-tiered players on the roster to be essential special teams players, though there was an extra emphasis from the Cardinals on the importance of that side of the ball.
Take in example Arizona keeping an eye-opening seven receivers . Three of their "lower tier" wideouts in Jalen Brooks, Simi Fehoko and Devin Duvernay all are projected to contribute heavily on fourth down.
"A lot of those competitions weren't necessarily against those guys [in the same position]. It was against other groups, and we thought that Jalen, Simi, some of those guys, obviously Duvernay is a returner, they provide in special teams at a high clip," LaFleur said.
Plenty can change from this roster, and with players such as James Conner and Tip Reiman on injured reserve, the complexion of each room can change when those respective guys are healthy.
With that said, the Cardinals were heavily projected to roll out 12 and 13 personnel, heavy tight end packages, often in 2026 in hopes of really establishing the run and getting the ground game going again.
Seven receivers, three tight ends and three running backs doesn't exactly back that belief up.
Arizona's thin at two essential positions to make those personnel groupings work on a weekly basis while seven receivers is more so used for 11 personnel.
The Cardinals were one of roughly five teams to roster seven receivers to begin the season. Out of those teams (Commanders, Rams, Dolphins, Panthers) Arizona ran the least amount of 11 personnel last season and the most multiple sets with tight ends.
Of course, you have to take that number with a grain of salt considering the Cardinals had a different head coach and offensive coordinator, though LaFleur's stint last year with Los Angeles saw the Rams pace the league with an eye-opening 31% usage of 13 personnel.
It will be truly interesting to see how the Cardinals deploy their offensive players this season, especially early while Conner and Reiman work their way back to health to supplement their respective positions.

title: Mike LaFleur Says The Quiet Part Out Loud About Arizona Cardinals Schedule
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals' 2026 schedule is fairly set and simple.
The Cardinals are one of five teams to not have any primetime games this coming season, joined by the Las Vegas Raiders, New York Jets, Miami Dolphins and Tennessee Titans.
Home or away, the Cardinals will be featured in the afternoon slate for all 17 matchups — which was a downgrade after having a Thursday Night Football and Monday Night Football battles in 2025.
Such is life when you finish with just three wins and restart with a new head coach. Losing franchise quarterback Kyler Murray certainly didn't help, either.
However, the Cardinals move forward with new coach Mike LaFleur in the saddle. LaFleur offers potential and hope for the organization entering the future, even if national audiences won't see it.
LaFleur's well aware of the task at hand — and why the Cardinals didn't get any love from execs across the various television networks.
"It sometimes gets choppy in terms of you love routine, and we got routine. We play 17 Sundays at the daytime, and I think we all understand why," LaFleur told reporters when breaking down the schedule.
"And if we want to play in those primetime slots and on Wednesdays and Thursdays and Netflix and all those kind of things, well, we got to go earn those spots. We understand that."
The Cardinals typically aren't viewed as ideal for television viewers. They've had just three primetime games in the last four seasons — counting 2026. The NFL does offer schedule flexing for possible big matchups to be moved to primetime, though the Cardinals aren't projected to be major players in the playoff race later in the season.
LaFleur drew the comparison to his brother Matt (who coaches the Green Bay Packers) when advancing his point.
"I think Green Bay, it's like they don't have like a seven-day stretch hardly at all. Their bye week is so twisted. They play on a Sunday, and then they have their bye week, but then they play the following Wednesday. So it's not even a bye week," said LaFleur. Green Bay has six primetime games scheduled this season.
"But then after they play Wednesday, they don't play till the following Sunday. So it's like the bye week's split in two. That's just the way this league is going. You better get used to it if you're a good football team. Hopefully, we have those issues moving forward."
Since moving into State Farm Stadium in 2006, the Cardinals haven't played more than four primetime games in a season. They have a .449 winning percentage since, which is tied for 23rd in the NFL.
Winning ultimately solves everything. LaFleur understands that, and to get the Cardinals back in somewhat of a national spotlight, he's got his work cut out for him.

title: Cardinals Biggest Roster Snubs—and Why They Should've Made the 53
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals officially have their initial 53-man roster and practice squad (mostly) set for the 2026 season.
It was a tough weekend for the Cardinals, who sent roughly 40% of their roster packing after weeks of evaluation in training camp and preseason . Deciding on a 53-man roster is never easy, regardless of the team or circumstance.
Truth be told, there wasn't a ton of true snubs from roster cuts — Arizona had a surplus of talent at various spots while the Cardinals suffered at others.
Still, these guys could have easily made the 53-man roster :
The Cardinals' wide receiver room truly felt like it was up for grabs for anybody to make the roster. Arizona stockpiled their room with seven total wideouts, and Smith-Marsette wasn't one.
Smith-Marsette was an early leader to make the team thanks to training camp playmaking and special teams/return prowess. However, Jalen Brooks and Simi Fehoko made the most of preseason opportunities.
Smith-Marsette barely missed out on the roster, and with the bottom of the barrel guys mostly needing to contribute on special teams, it felt like Smith-Marsette was the better solution over Brooks in that aspect.
Even then, it's understandable why Brooks was kept.
This was a massive vote of confidence in Garrett Williams' achilles being fully healthy.
Murphy-Bunting has six prior years of experience in the league, which paced the Cardinals' cornerback room by multiple seasons. His versatility and recent move to the slot also played in his favor, though he lost out to Kei'Trel Clark and Max Melton among the others.
Perhaps this was a move based off youth/potential, which makes sense. Murphy-Bunting also missed last season with an offseason ACL injury. However, he was one of the biggest names that was sent packing before ultimately landing in Tampa Bay on their practice squad.
Hull was a late push for a potential roster spot, and his final audition in Green Bay was undoubtedly his greatest. In a Cardinals offense that will run the ball, and hopefully often, Arizona surprisingly only kept three players at the position — even with a banged up Jeremiyah Love and James Conner/Trey Benson on injured reserve.
Hull clearly showed a capability to succeed in LaFleur's system. He was brought back to the practice squad and could very well be elevated to the roster throughout the season, though Arizona surprisingly omitted a fourth running back from the list with Hull touted as fans' biggest name that missed out.
Thomas was projected to be the team's starting cornerback before his season-ending ACL injury last training camp. Thomas recovered, though players typically take a full year of play time before they return to their normal selves.
Unfortunately, the Cardinals' efforts to bolster the cornerback room within recent years led to a logjam, where some sort of talent was going to fall through the cracks. That happened to be Thomas, who was on the outside looking in of a surprisingly small cornerback room of five.
Granted, he re-signed on the practice squad, so it's not as if the Cardinals completely gave up on him — though if he can make a full recovery, Thomas' play is worthy of a roster spot.
The Cardinals are suspected to run plenty of heavy tight end personnel packages, so the prevailing thought was Arizona would at least keep four players at the position. With Tip Reiman likely heading to PUP/reserve (which he ultimately did), there was a need for another run-blocking presence.
All of which set up Quitoriano to at least make the initial 53-man roster — though that wasn't the case as the Cardinals traded for Hunter Long and only carried three tight ends into the season with Reiman out.
Quitoriano isn't an all-star tight end, though he's a viable blocker and could have easily made it through. He ended up re-signing on the practice squad.
